title: Multiple Testing: Simultaneous Metric Evaluation
description: A growth team at an e-commerce company runs an A/B test on a new checkout flow and tracks 12 metrics simultaneously — activation rate, D1 retention, D7 retention, session length, feature engagement, NPS proxy, support tickets, revenue per user, and four funnel conversion steps. The test runs for 14 days and returns p < 0.05 on three metrics. The team declares success on all three and ships the feature. What is the primary statistical error in this workflow?
options: The test ran too long, inflating the Type II error rate across all metrics
Testing 12 metrics simultaneously inflates the family-wise Type I error rate far above 5%, so some significant results are likely false positives
The team should have used a one-tailed test for each metric to reduce the number of comparisons
D1 and D7 retention are correlated, so they should be counted as a single metric
explanation: When testing 12 metrics at α=0.05, the probability of at least one false positive is 1-(0.95)^12 ≈ 46%, far above the intended 5% threshold. This is the multiple comparisons problem, and corrections such as adjusting the per-test alpha or controlling the false discovery rate are needed. Pre-registering a single primary metric before the experiment starts is the cleanest solution. Running longer (option A) affects power to detect real effects, not the Type I error rate — a longer test would not fix spurious positives. One-tailed tests (option C) reduce power and change directional sensitivity but do not address the multiple-comparisons issue at all. Metric correlation (option D) is a real secondary concern but the primary flaw is the uncorrected family-wise error rate, not correlation per se.
hints: Think about what happens to the overall false positive rate when you run many simultaneous significance tests.
If each test has a 5% chance of a false positive independently, what is the probability of at least one false positive across all 12 tests?
concepts: TYPE I AND TYPE II ERRORS

title: Sample Ratio Mismatch Detection
description: A SaaS company runs an A/B test splitting traffic 50/50 between a new onboarding flow (treatment) and the existing flow (control). After two weeks, the data team notices that control has 48,200 users and treatment has 41,900 users — a 13% shortfall. The engineer insists the randomization code looked correct and the experiment should be analyzed as-is. What is the most appropriate response to this discrepancy?
options: Proceed with analysis but weight the treatment group to match control size
The imbalance is within acceptable sampling variance and no action is needed
Stop the experiment, investigate the assignment pipeline for bugs, and do not trust the results until the imbalance is explained
Analyze only the first week of data when traffic was presumably more balanced
explanation: A 13% shortfall in one arm — roughly 6,300 users — is far outside the variance expected from random chance with a 50/50 split. This pattern, called a sample ratio mismatch, almost always indicates a systematic bug in the assignment, logging, or filtering pipeline. The results are not trustworthy because the two groups likely differ on dimensions beyond the treatment itself — any measured effect could be an artifact of who was lost. Simply weighting (option A) does not fix the underlying selection bias and may make inference worse. Sampling variance alone (option B) cannot explain a 13% gap at this scale — a chi-square test on the assignment counts would yield an astronomically small p-value. Analyzing only week one (option D) still uses data from a broken pipeline and does not diagnose what went wrong.
hints: Large, systematic imbalances between groups suggest something went wrong before the analysis, not during it.
Ask yourself: could random coin-flipping produce this big a split across 90,000 users?

title: Novelty Effect in Feature Launch
description: A consumer app launches a new personalized feed algorithm in a two-week A/B test. Treatment users show a 12% lift in daily sessions compared to control. The team is excited and prepares to ship. A senior data scientist warns that the measured lift may be artificially high due to a novelty effect. Which of the following best describes the novelty effect concern and the appropriate mitigation?
options: New users in treatment may have different baseline engagement, so the team should segment by user tenure

Users in the new feed condition may engage more simply because it is unfamiliar and novel, not because it is genuinely better — a longer test period or new-user-only analysis would help assess persistence
The 12% lift may be due to seasonal trends, so the team should run the test during a non-peak period
Personalization algorithms cause self-reinforcing feedback loops, so the test should be rerun with a stratified sample
explanation: The novelty effect occurs when users engage more with a new experience simply because it is different or interesting, not because it delivers lasting value. This inflates short-term metrics and can cause a team to ship a change that eventually decays to zero or negative lift once the novelty wears off. Mitigations include running the experiment long enough for engagement to stabilize, or looking specifically at users who have been in treatment long enough that novelty should have worn off. Segmenting by user tenure (option A) addresses a real confound but is not the novelty effect — tenure controls for lifecycle differences, not behavioral inflation from newness. Seasonal trends (option C) affect both arms equally in a concurrent A/B test, so they do not create the specific novelty distortion. Feedback loops in personalization (option D) are a real concern for long-run validity but describe a different problem — not the short-term inflation the senior scientist is worried about.
hints: Consider whether the engagement lift comes from the feature being better or merely from being new and unfamiliar.
Think about how engagement might evolve over time if users simply get used to the new experience.

title: Statistical Power and Sample Size Trade-off
description: A marketplace company wants to detect a 2% lift in gross merchandise value (GMV) per user with 80% power at α=0.05. The initial power calculation suggests 200,000 users per arm are needed. The business team, eager to ship, proposes cutting the test to 50,000 users per arm to save time. The data scientist pushes back. Which consequence correctly describes running the underpowered test?
options: The test will have a higher Type I error rate, increasing the chance of false positives
The test will have lower power, meaning true effects of 2% GMV lift are more likely to go undetected
The reduced sample will make the test more sensitive because noise is lower with fewer users
The confidence intervals will be narrower, making it easier to detect the 2% effect
explanation: Statistical power is the probability of detecting a true effect when one exists. Reducing the sample size from 200,000 to 50,000 per arm dramatically lowers power — likely from 80% to below 40% for a 2% GMV effect. This means the team would miss real improvements most of the time, wasting test cycles. The Type I error rate (option A) is controlled by the significance threshold α=0.05, which is independent of sample size — the false positive rate does not change. With fewer users, statistical noise per estimate is actually higher, not lower (option C) — the standard error of the mean increases as n shrinks. Confidence intervals become wider, not narrower (option D), with fewer observations, making it harder to resolve small effects.
hints: Power and sample size move in the same direction — cutting one cuts the other.
Think about which error type (missing a real effect vs. declaring a false one) is affected by sample size alone.
concepts: TYPE I AND TYPE II ERRORS

title: Choosing the Right Primary Metric
description: A social media platform is testing a new notification digest feature that consolidates push notifications into a daily summary. The product team proposes using 'notification open rate' as the primary success metric. A data scientist argues this metric is a poor primary metric for this experiment. Which argument best supports the data scientist's concern?
options: Open rate is too easy to manipulate and will give the treatment an unfair advantage
Open rate directly measures the treatment's mechanism, so it is the ideal metric

Notification open rate measures intermediate engagement with the digest but may miss downstream user value metrics like session starts or content consumption, and it is mechanically altered by the feature itself
Open rate is not a ratio metric and should be converted to an absolute count before analysis
explanation: Notification open rate is a 'local' metric that is mechanically tied to the feature being tested — the digest consolidates notifications, so naturally the number of opens and the denominator change, making comparison to control ambiguous. More importantly, it does not capture whether users actually benefit: a user who opens the digest but then leaves the app has a high open rate but poor downstream value. The primary metric in an experiment should reflect the true business or user outcome — for a notification feature, this is more likely session starts, content interactions, or retention. Option A misunderstands manipulation — the issue is not gaming but metric misalignment. Option B is the trap: just because open rate is mechanically tied to the change does not make it the right primary metric. Option D is a misconception; ratios and rates are perfectly valid primary metrics.
hints: Ask whether the metric you're measuring reflects true user value or just surface-level interaction with the feature.
Consider whether the feature changes the definition or denominator of the metric itself.

title: Network Effects and Interference
description: A ride-sharing marketplace is testing a new driver incentive program that offers bonuses for completing rides in high-demand zones. The experiment assigns 50% of drivers to the treatment (incentive) and 50% to control. After three weeks, treatment drivers complete 8% more rides. However, the data team suspects the true effect is overstated. What is the most likely cause?
options: Treatment drivers tend to have newer vehicles, introducing a confound
The incentive causes treatment drivers to cluster in high-demand zones, reducing ride availability for control drivers — the control group is harmed by the treatment, inflating the measured effect
Three weeks is too short to observe the full effect of an incentive program
Drivers who opt into the incentive are self-selected, so the experiment is not randomized
explanation: This is a classic network effects / market interference problem. In a two-sided marketplace, treatment and control users share the same supply and demand pool. When treatment drivers cluster in high-demand zones, they capture rides that would have gone to control drivers. This means control performance is artificially depressed — the measured gap between treatment and control overstates the true effect that would be observed if the entire fleet used the incentive. The correct approach is to randomize at a geographic or market level, not at the individual driver level. Vehicle quality (option A) is a plausible confound in observational studies but not in a properly randomized experiment. Test duration (option C) is a real concern for novelty effects but not for interference. Option D is wrong — the experiment was randomized; the issue is that the units of randomization (individual drivers) violate the independence assumption because they interact through the same marketplace.
hints: Think about whether the control group is truly isolated from the treatment, or whether the two groups share a common resource.
In a marketplace, treatment and control units often compete for the same supply or demand.

title: Variance Reduction with Pre-experiment Covariates
description: An e-commerce company is testing a new product recommendation algorithm. Revenue per user has extremely high variance due to a small number of large purchasers. The data scientist proposes using each user's pre-experiment revenue as a covariate to reduce variance in the treatment effect estimate. The product manager questions whether this is necessary. Which response best justifies the variance reduction approach?
options: Using pre-experiment data introduces look-ahead bias and will invalidate the causal inference

By conditioning on pre-experiment revenue, the method reduces residual variance in the outcome, allowing the same sample to detect smaller effects or run for a shorter duration while maintaining 80% power
Pre-experiment revenue is correlated with treatment assignment, so including it will reduce bias rather than variance
Variance reduction techniques only work when the metric is normally distributed, so they are not appropriate for revenue data
explanation: Using pre-experiment outcomes as covariates is a well-established method for reducing variance in experiment estimates. Because a user's past revenue is a strong predictor of future revenue, conditioning on it explains a large share of outcome variability. The resulting estimate has smaller standard errors, which translates directly into higher power — you can detect the same effect with fewer users, or detect smaller effects with the same sample. Pre-experiment data is fine to use as a covariate because it was collected before treatment assignment, so it cannot be caused by the treatment (no look-ahead bias, option A is wrong). In a properly randomized experiment, pre-experiment revenue is uncorrelated with treatment assignment — so including it reduces variance, not bias (option C is wrong). Option D is a misconception; variance reduction via covariate adjustment works even when the outcome is non-normal, though the efficiency gains vary.
hints: If you can predict a user's outcome before the experiment starts, that predictive power can be used to reduce unexplained noise in the estimate.
Think about what 'residual variance' means — variance the treatment assignment alone cannot explain.

title: Segmentation Analysis and Simpson's Paradox
description: A SaaS platform runs an A/B test on a new pricing page. Overall, conversion rate is 5.2% for control and 5.1% for treatment — a non-significant difference. A curious analyst breaks results by plan tier: among monthly subscribers, treatment converts at 6.1% vs control's 5.5%; among annual subscribers, treatment converts at 3.8% vs control's 4.2%. Both segments favor opposite directions. The overall result is neutral because annual subscribers dominate the sample. What should the team conclude?
options: The test is conclusive — overall non-significance means the feature has no effect and should not be shipped
The segment-level differences are likely noise because the overall test was not significant
The heterogeneous effects suggest the feature may help monthly subscribers but hurt annual ones — the team should investigate whether the pricing page is appropriate for both segments before deciding
The analyst should combine both segments into one group and re-run the significance test to get a definitive answer
explanation: This is a case of aggregation masking heterogeneous treatment effects — an effect that is positive in one subgroup and negative in another can cancel out in the overall average. The overall non-significance does not mean there is no effect; it means the average effect across a mixed population is near zero. The correct next step is to take the segment-level findings seriously as a hypothesis for further investigation, ideally with pre-registered subgroup analysis to avoid false discovery. Declaring no effect (option A) ignores the segment-level evidence and could mean missing a real opportunity for monthly users. Dismissing the segments as noise (option B) is premature — subgroup effects can be real even when the overall p-value is not significant, especially when the groups have opposite directions. Re-combining and re-testing (option D) just reproduces the same overall analysis that already ran and would not resolve the heterogeneity.
hints: Overall averages can hide opposite effects in different subgroups — look at whether the composition of your sample drives the aggregate result.
When effects differ by segment, ask whether a single combined answer is even the right question.

title: Experiment Duration and Weekly Seasonality
description: A consumer app team runs an A/B test on a new home screen layout starting on a Tuesday and ending the following Monday — exactly seven days. The test shows a 4% improvement in weekly active users. A data scientist flags that the test duration may be problematic. What is the most valid concern?
options: Seven days is always too short to observe any statistically significant effect

A seven-day test starting on Tuesday ends on Monday, meaning it does not cover a full Monday-through-Sunday week — weekend and weekday behavior differ, and different start/end days can produce biased estimates if one arm happened to capture more weekend traffic
Seven-day tests always suffer from novelty effects and should be extended to 30 days
The test should have started on a Monday to align with standard business reporting cycles
explanation: User behavior varies significantly by day of week — weekday users may use an app for productivity while weekend users browse recreationally. A test that does not cover a whole number of full calendar weeks can produce biased results if the assignment happens to over-represent certain days in one arm. Running from Tuesday to Monday means the final partial week is handled differently by each arm if traffic drifts. Best practice is to run for complete week increments (7, 14, 21 days) starting and ending on the same weekday. Seven days is not always too short (option A) — it depends on the effect size and traffic volume. Novelty effects (option C) are a real concern but are not universally solved by 30-day tests, and 7 days is sometimes sufficient. Starting on Monday (option D) addresses reporting aesthetics, not the statistical validity of the duration.
hints: Think about how user behavior patterns differ across the days of the week and what that means for a test that starts mid-week.
Consider whether the start and end days of a test affect which types of behavior are over- or under-represented.

title: Sample Ratio Mismatch from Logging Bug
description: A social media platform runs a 50/50 A/B test on a new video autoplay feature. After one week, the analytics dashboard shows 210,000 users in control and 163,000 in treatment. The engineer explains that the logging pipeline for treatment events had a 5-hour outage on day 3 but otherwise worked fine. The product manager suggests proceeding with the analysis using available data. What is the primary risk of this approach?
options: The 5-hour outage means the test ran for only 6.5 days instead of 7, reducing power slightly

Users whose events were lost during the outage are systematically missing from treatment data — if these users have different engagement patterns, the treatment group is biased and results are not comparable to control
Logging outages only affect impression data, not conversion data, so the analysis can proceed on conversion metrics
The analysis should be restricted to users who joined the experiment before the outage began
explanation: When events are missing due to a logging outage, the missingness is not random — it affects only treatment users during a specific time window. If those hours had higher or lower engagement (e.g., a weekday evening spike), the treatment sample is no longer representative. Users whose data was dropped are effectively excluded from the treatment arm but not from control, creating a selection bias. The resulting comparison is between a complete control group and a selectively-logged treatment group. Option A underestimates the problem — it is not just a power reduction but a structural bias. Option C is wrong; logging outages affect all event types, and even if conversion data were unaffected, the denominator (who is counted as a user) would be wrong. Option D sounds reasonable but still uses data from a broken pipeline and does not restore the missing treatment users.
hints: Ask whether the missing data is missing at random, or whether it is systematically tied to a specific user group or time window.
A logging gap that affects only one arm creates different data quality in treatment vs. control.

title: Type I Error and Repeated Peeking
description: A growth analyst at an e-commerce company checks the experiment dashboard every morning and stops the test the moment it crosses p < 0.05. The test was planned for 14 days but was stopped on day 6. The team ships the feature. What fundamental error occurred in this process?
options: Stopping the test early increases the chance of a Type II error by reducing sample size
Repeated significance testing without correction inflates the Type I error rate — peeking daily at a 14-day test can push the effective false positive rate well above 5%
The test should have run longer to capture novelty effect decay before stopping
Shipping after six days violates the pre-registered stopping rule, which is an ethical violation but does not affect statistical validity
explanation: This is the peeking problem, a well-documented inflation of Type I error. When you test repeatedly on accumulating data and stop at the first significant result, you exploit random fluctuations in the p-value trajectory. Simulations show that peeking daily on a fixed test can push the effective false positive rate from 5% to 20–30% or higher over a 14-day window. The correct approaches are sequential testing methods (which formally control error under optional stopping) or simply committing to a fixed sample size before peeking. Option A is partially true — early stopping does reduce sample size and can affect power — but that is a secondary concern; the primary flaw is the inflated false positive rate. Novelty effect decay (option C) is a separate concern about the experiment lasting long enough for effects to stabilize, not about the stopping rule. Option D is wrong: the statistical invalidity is the central problem, not just an ethical issue.
hints: Think about what happens to the overall probability of a false positive when you check results many times during a single test.
Consider the trajectory of a p-value under the null hypothesis — it will occasionally dip below 0.05 even when there is no real effect.
concepts: TYPE I AND TYPE II ERRORS

title: Network Effects in Social Features
description: A messaging app tests a new group chat feature by randomly assigning individual users to treatment (access to the feature) and control (no access). After four weeks, treatment users send 15% more messages per day. The experiment team is about to declare success. A researcher raises a concern about the validity of the individual-level randomization. What is the researcher most likely concerned about?
options: Individual randomization is the gold standard and should not be questioned

Users in treatment and control may be in the same social networks — when a treatment user creates a group chat, control users who are invited to that chat are exposed to the feature, contaminating the control group
The 15% lift in messages per day is likely driven by power users in treatment, and the analysis should be restricted to median users
Four weeks is too long for a messaging feature test and the results include novelty decay
explanation: Group chat is an inherently social feature — its value depends on network connections. When individual users within the same social graph are assigned to different conditions, treatment users inevitably interact with control users. A control user invited to a group chat created by a treatment user is partially exposed to the feature, violating the assumption that control is untouched. This network spillover deflates the observed treatment effect (if control users partly benefit) or inflates it (if being excluded from chats they can see makes control users less active). The correct design is to randomize at the network cluster level — by friend group or geographic community. Option A is wrong for social features where user behavior is interdependent. Option C identifies a power-user concern but is not the researcher's main point. Option D misapplies the novelty concern — four weeks is often appropriate for social features to settle.
hints: For social or collaborative features, ask whether treatment and control users interact with each other.
If users in different experiment arms can influence each other's behavior, the independence assumption of standard A/B testing breaks down.

title: Confidence Interval Interpretation
description: A marketplace runs an A/B test on a new seller dashboard. The primary metric is seller revenue per week. After three weeks with 5,000 sellers per arm, the analysis yields a treatment effect estimate of +$42 per seller per week with a 95% confidence interval of [$18, $66]. The product team asks: 'Can we say there is a 95% probability that the true effect is between $18 and $66?' What is the statistically correct answer?
options: Yes — the 95% confidence interval directly gives a 95% probability that the true effect falls in that range

No — the interval is a frequentist construct meaning that if the experiment were repeated many times, 95% of such intervals would contain the true fixed effect; we cannot make probabilistic statements about the specific interval
No — the 95% refers to the power of the test, not the probability the true effect is in range
Yes, but only if the data is normally distributed, which revenue data typically is not
explanation: The frequentist 95% confidence interval is commonly misinterpreted as a probability statement about the true parameter. The correct interpretation is: under repeated sampling and interval construction, 95% of such intervals would contain the true (fixed) parameter. Once the interval is observed ($18 to $66), the true effect is either in it or not — there is no probability to assign to a fixed interval containing a fixed number. This is a subtle but important distinction in statistical communication. Option A states the popular but incorrect interpretation. Option C confuses the confidence level with power, which are entirely different concepts. Option D correctly notes that revenue is not normally distributed, but confidence interval validity is guaranteed asymptotically by the central limit theorem at n=5,000 per arm — the normality of the data is not required for the interval to be valid.
hints: In frequentist statistics, the parameter is fixed and the interval is random — not the other way around.
Think about what '95%' refers to: the procedure over many repetitions, or the specific interval in front of you.

title: Holdout Groups for Long-Run Measurement
description: A SaaS company ships a new AI-powered search feature to all users after a successful two-week A/B test. Three months later, a stakeholder asks whether the feature is still delivering value. The data team realizes they have no way to measure the ongoing impact because the control group was turned off at ship time. What should the team have done differently?
options: Run a post-hoc survey asking users to estimate how much the feature helps them
Maintain a small holdout group — typically 1–5% of users who never received the feature — so that ongoing causal impact can be measured months after the initial ship
Use the pre-ship historical data as the counterfactual baseline for post-ship measurement
Re-run the A/B test three months later with a fresh cohort
explanation: A holdout group is a permanent or long-running control population that does not receive shipped features, allowing the team to measure causal impact well beyond the initial test window. This is especially valuable for features where novelty effects are a concern or where long-run engagement dynamics differ from short-run responses. Surveys (option A) rely on self-reporting and cannot isolate the feature's causal contribution from other concurrent changes. Using pre-ship historical data (option C) is an interrupted time series approach that is vulnerable to confounds — any other change that occurred at ship time will contaminate the estimate. Re-running an A/B test three months later (option D) measures the incremental effect of turning the feature on again for new users, not the long-run effect of the original ship.
hints: Once everyone has a feature, there is no clean comparison group left — think about how to preserve one.
Long-run measurement requires a causal comparison that is concurrent, not historical.

title: Segmentation Analysis: New vs. Returning Users
description: A consumer app tests a redesigned home screen. Overall, the test shows a neutral result (p=0.31). An analyst segments by user type and finds that new users (first 7 days) show a statistically significant 9% increase in D7 retention in treatment, while returning users (>30 days tenure) show a non-significant -2% change. The team debates whether to ship to new users only. What is the most important statistical caveat before acting on this segment finding?
options: Segment findings are always reliable if the segment-level p-value is below 0.05

Because the segment analysis was not pre-registered as a primary analysis, it may be a false positive inflated by multiple subgroup tests — it should be treated as a hypothesis to validate in a targeted follow-up experiment
The -2% change for returning users confirms there is no effect for that segment, so shipping to new users only is safe
The 9% lift for new users is too large to be real — it should be discarded as an outlier
explanation: Post-hoc subgroup analyses carry a high risk of false positives because the analyst is implicitly running multiple comparisons across segments. Finding a significant result in one segment after the overall test was neutral is exactly the pattern you would expect from chance alone when testing multiple groups. The correct approach is to treat the new-user finding as a hypothesis and validate it in a dedicated experiment pre-specified for new users. Option A is wrong — a segment p-value below 0.05 does not correct for the multiple comparisons made across segments. Option C incorrectly treats the null result for returning users as confirmatory — not rejecting a hypothesis is not the same as confirming it. Option D is the opposite error — the 9% lift should not be discarded but rather validated, not dismissed.
hints: When you test multiple subgroups, each one is an additional opportunity for a false positive — the same rules that apply to metric families apply to segment families.
A significant finding in one subgroup after an overall null result is a hypothesis, not a conclusion.

title: Sample Ratio Mismatch from Eligibility Filter
description: An e-commerce company runs a 50/50 A/B test on a new checkout button style. After analysis, control has 95,000 sessions and treatment has 102,000 sessions — a 7.4% surplus in treatment. The engineer says the randomization hash uses session ID and should be perfectly balanced. The analyst suspects an eligibility filter applied after randomization is causing the imbalance. How would a post-randomization eligibility filter cause a sample ratio mismatch?
options: The eligibility filter would increase both arms proportionally and would not cause a mismatch

If the filter criteria correlate with treatment assignment — for example, if the filter uses a feature that is only triggered by the treatment experience — then treatment and control lose different proportions of sessions, breaking balance
Post-randomization filters always cause sample ratio mismatches and should never be used
The 7.4% surplus is within acceptable variance for session-level randomization
explanation: A sample ratio mismatch caused by a post-randomization filter arises when the filter's inclusion/exclusion criteria are correlated with the assignment. For example, if the new checkout button triggers a page reload that changes the session ID, or if the eligibility check itself is only shown to users who interact with the button (treatment users), then a higher proportion of treatment sessions pass the filter compared to control. The filter must be truly independent of treatment assignment to be safe. Option A is correct only if the filter is perfectly independent of assignment — which may not hold in practice. Option C is too strong — post-randomization filters are valid when designed carefully, but they require scrutiny. Option D is wrong — at ~200,000 total sessions, a 7,000-session imbalance is statistically impossible from random chance and must be investigated.
hints: Think about whether the event or condition used by the filter could itself be triggered differently in treatment vs. control.
If the filter behaves differently based on what users see, it is no longer independent of assignment.

title: Novelty Effect Diagnosis via Cohort Analysis
description: A productivity SaaS tool ships a new AI writing assistant in an A/B test. Week-over-week, the treatment group shows declining engagement uplift: +18% in week 1, +11% in week 2, +6% in week 3, +3% in week 4. Control engagement is flat across all four weeks. The product manager argues the feature is still positive (still above zero) and should be shipped. The data scientist is less confident. Which analysis would most directly help diagnose whether this is a novelty effect?
options: Segment treatment users by engagement level in week 1 — high engagers will show more novelty effect decay

Look at treatment users who have been in the experiment for 4+ weeks and measure their engagement trend compared to equivalent long-tenure control users — if the gap is converging toward zero, novelty decay is likely
Extend the test to 8 weeks to see if the positive effect stabilizes or reaches zero
Compare the week 4 engagement level in treatment to the week 1 engagement level in control as the baseline
explanation: The most direct diagnosis of novelty effect is a within-experiment cohort analysis: take users who have been in treatment for the longest time and examine whether their relative advantage over equivalent long-tenure control users is shrinking. If early-cohort treatment users no longer show meaningful lift by week 4, the effect is decaying rather than genuine. This provides causal evidence within the current experiment without requiring a longer run. Option A segments by week-1 engagement level, which captures heterogeneity in adoption but does not directly measure temporal decay due to novelty. Extending to 8 weeks (option C) is a reasonable approach but is slower and provides the same information with a delay — the cohort analysis within existing data is faster. Option D creates a confounded comparison — week 4 treatment users have a different experience from week 1 control users for many reasons beyond novelty, so this comparison is not valid.
hints: Novelty-driven benefit is largest when the feature is newest to the user — and should fade as users habituate. How would you look for that fading pattern in a cohort-level view of the treatment effect over time?
Focus on long-tenure treatment users rather than the aggregate to isolate the time-in-experiment dimension.

title: Multiple Testing with Sequential Feature Rollouts
description: A product team ships three features in quick succession over six weeks, each evaluated with a separate A/B test at α=0.05. Feature A: p=0.03. Feature B: p=0.04. Feature C: p=0.048. All three are declared significant and shipped. A statistician reviews the process and raises a concern about the combined inference. What is the statistician's concern?
options: Each test was run at the correct α level, so there is no statistical issue with the sequential approach
Running three independent tests each at α=0.05 means the probability of at least one false positive across the three is approximately 14%, not 5% — some findings may be spurious
Sequential tests should use a one-tailed hypothesis to maintain power across multiple evaluations
The features should have been tested simultaneously in a multivariate test rather than sequentially
explanation: Three independent tests each at α=0.05 have a family-wise false positive rate of 1-(1-0.05)^3 ≈ 14.3%. If the team is implicitly asking 'did any of these features work?' and declaring each significant result a success, the collective false positive rate is well above 5%. This is analogous to the simultaneous testing problem but across sequential tests that share a common decision context. If the three tests are truly independent decisions with no shared interpretation, the multiplicity concern is weaker — but in practice, teams frame sequential results together. Option A ignores the family-wise inflation. Sequential tests should generally use lower per-test alpha or an overall error budget, not one-tailed tests (option C) — one-tailed tests reduce sensitivity to negative effects and do not address multiplicity. Simultaneous multivariate testing (option D) has its own statistical challenges and is not clearly superior to sequential testing for independent features.
hints: Think about whether the company cares about whether 'any' of its experiments found something true, or whether 'all' of them did.
If you roll a die three times, the chance of getting a 6 at least once is higher than on a single roll.
concepts: TYPE I AND TYPE II ERRORS

title: Variance Reduction via Metric Transformation
description: An e-commerce platform measures revenue per user as its primary experiment metric. The distribution is extremely right-skewed — 1% of users generate 40% of revenue. A data scientist proposes using log(revenue + 1) as the metric instead, arguing it will reduce variance and improve test sensitivity. A colleague argues this changes what you are measuring and introduces interpretation problems. Who is more correct, and why?
options: The data scientist is correct — log transformation always reduces variance and should always be applied to revenue metrics

The colleague is more correct — transforming the metric changes the estimand from mean revenue to mean log-revenue, which may not align with the business objective, and a better approach is to use robust variance estimation or winsorization
The data scientist is correct because log revenue is equivalent to revenue when the effect is small
Both are wrong — the correct solution is to exclude the top 1% of users as outliers before analysis
explanation: Log transformation does reduce variance for right-skewed distributions, but it changes the quantity being estimated. The mean of log(revenue) is not the same as the log of mean revenue — the geometric mean differs from the arithmetic mean. If the business cares about total revenue impact, the arithmetic mean is the right estimand, and log-transforming the metric makes the result harder to interpret in business terms. Better alternatives for handling high-variance revenue metrics include winsorization (capping extreme values at a percentile) or using pre-experiment revenue as a covariate. Option A overstates the value of log transformation — it helps variance but at the cost of estimand clarity. Option C is wrong — for skewed outcomes, the effect on log-revenue and the effect on revenue can diverge substantially. Option D — excluding the top 1% — introduces bias by systematically removing the highest-value users, and the impact on the business metric is not symmetric.
hints: When you transform a metric, ask whether the transformed metric still answers the business question you care about.
There is a difference between reducing statistical noise and changing what you are estimating.

title: Cluster Randomization for Network Features
description: A professional social network wants to test a new 'mutual connection recommendations' feature. Individual-level randomization is proposed: 50% of users see the feature, 50% do not. A senior researcher argues that individual-level randomization is inappropriate for this feature. What is the primary reason, and what is the better design?
options: Individual randomization is appropriate because it maximizes statistical power by treating each user independently

Individual randomization causes interference: a treatment user may recommend someone who is in control, and the control user benefits from the recommendation without being in treatment — inflating or deflating measured effects. Randomizing at the network cluster level (e.g., geographic region or community) would isolate spillovers
The feature is too complex to test in an A/B framework and should be evaluated using surveys
Individual randomization is fine but the test should run for 60 days to reduce novelty effects from recommendation novelty
explanation: Mutual connection recommendations create a direct dependency between users — a recommendation from a treatment user can reach a control user and drive value or behavior change for the control user. This violates the Stable Unit Treatment Value Assumption (SUTVA) required for valid causal inference in individual-level randomization. The recommended design is to randomize at the cluster level — by geographic market, friend community, or organizational network — so that users within a cluster share the same treatment condition and spillovers stay within the cluster. This reduces power (clusters have fewer effective observations than individuals) but is necessary for validity. Option A is correct that individual randomization maximizes power, but it sacrifices validity, which is a more fundamental requirement. Surveys (option C) cannot replace a causal experiment for a feature at this scale. Extending to 60 days (option D) addresses novelty but does not solve the interference problem.
hints: For features where users interact with each other, ask whether a control user can be reached by a treatment user's actions.
The level at which you randomize should match the level at which interference can propagate.

title: Minimum Detectable Effect and Business Threshold
description: A marketplace platform calculates that with its current daily traffic, a 21-day A/B test at 80% power and α=0.05 can detect a minimum detectable effect (MDE) of 3% in checkout conversion. The product team believes the new checkout redesign will lift conversion by 1%. The business case requires at least a 1% lift to justify the development cost. How should the team proceed?
options: Run the 21-day test — if p > 0.05, conclude the feature does not work

The test is underpowered for the expected effect size — options include increasing traffic allocation, extending duration, or accepting that the expected 1% lift cannot be reliably measured with current traffic
Run the test for 7 days at a higher alpha (e.g., α=0.15) to increase power
Use a one-tailed test to effectively double the power for detecting positive effects only
explanation: When the MDE of a test (3%) is larger than the expected true effect (1%), the test is underpowered for the business-relevant effect size. Running the test and calling it null if p > 0.05 would be a common mistake — it would have low probability of detecting the real 1% effect even if it exists. The right responses are to increase sample size (more traffic, longer duration) until the MDE drops to or below 1%, or to explicitly acknowledge that this effect cannot be reliably measured and make a qualitative decision. Running at higher alpha (option C) increases the false positive rate without solving the power problem — it trades one error type for another rather than fixing the fundamental sensitivity issue. A one-tailed test (option D) does modestly increase power for one direction, but the gain is not enough to bridge the gap from 3% MDE to 1% MDE and also removes ability to detect negative effects.
hints: The MDE tells you the smallest effect your test can reliably find — if the expected effect is below the MDE, the test will miss it most of the time.
When the expected effect is smaller than what you can detect, you have three options: get more data, accept lower confidence, or decide without the experiment.

title: Debug: Carryover Bias in Sequential Testing
description: A SaaS company uses the same user cohort for three consecutive A/B tests over six months: first testing a pricing page, then an onboarding flow, then an email cadence. Users are randomly reassigned to treatment or control for each new test. A data scientist reviewing the results suspects that the second and third tests may be biased. What is the most likely source of bias?
options: Random reassignment between tests is unnecessary and introduces statistical noise

Users who experienced the treatment in test 1 may have permanently changed their behavior (e.g., upgraded their plan or changed usage patterns), so their baseline in tests 2 and 3 differs from users who were always in control — causing carryover contamination
Using the same users repeatedly increases statistical power because the variance is lower for a panel than a cross-section
The tests should have been run simultaneously to avoid seasonal confounds
explanation: Carryover bias occurs when exposure to a prior treatment permanently or persistently changes a user's state, so that their behavior in subsequent tests reflects the earlier treatment rather than a clean baseline. For example, if users who saw the treatment pricing page in test 1 converted to a higher-tier plan, their revenue in tests 2 and 3 is permanently different — they are no longer exchangeable with control users from test 1. Random reassignment between tests does not fix this because the users' underlying states have changed. Option A is wrong — random reassignment between tests is good practice; it is the carryover in user state that is the issue. Option C correctly notes that repeated measurement of the same users can reduce variance, but this does not offset the carryover bias concern. Option D is a separate concern; simultaneous testing has its own challenges and does not eliminate carryover from prior experiments.
hints: Think about whether users who experienced a prior treatment are truly comparable to users who did not, even after re-randomization.
Some behavioral changes from experiments are persistent — a user who upgraded a plan stays on that plan.

title: Bayesian Experimentation: Early Stopping
description: A consumer app product team uses a Bayesian A/B testing framework. After five days, the posterior probability that treatment is better than control is 97%. The team wants to stop the experiment and ship. A frequentist colleague warns against early stopping. The product manager asks the data scientist to explain whether early stopping is more permissible in a Bayesian framework. What is the correct explanation?
options: Bayesian frameworks are always equivalent to frequentist ones, so early stopping is equally problematic in both

Bayesian methods that use proper stopping rules (e.g., stopping when the posterior exceeds a threshold) can be valid under optional stopping, unlike frequentist p-values which inflate under repeated testing — but the Bayesian conclusion still depends on the prior and may overstate certainty with small samples
Because the posterior is 97%, the team can be 97% confident the true effect is positive and stop immediately
Early stopping is invalid in all experimental frameworks and the test must always run to the planned sample size
explanation: Bayesian inference has the technical property of being coherent under optional stopping — the posterior probability at any point is a valid statement of belief given the data seen so far, without the multiple-testing inflation that afflicts frequentist p-values. However, this does not mean stopping is without risk: with small samples, the posterior can be heavily influenced by the prior, and if the prior is misspecified, the 97% credibility may overstate true confidence. Additionally, practical issues like novelty effects and seasonality still apply. The frequentist concern (option A) about p-value inflation does not directly transfer to Bayesian posteriors, so they are not equivalent in this regard. Option C is the common misinterpretation of Bayesian credible intervals as probability statements about the true parameter — while more defensible in a Bayesian framework than in frequentist, it still requires careful wording. Option D is too absolute — sequential and Bayesian designs explicitly allow for principled early stopping.
hints: Frequentist p-values drift over time when you peek repeatedly — Bayesian posteriors have different mathematical properties in this regard.
Even in a Bayesian framework, ask whether small sample size and prior choice might be driving the strong posterior.

title: Experiment Duration: Long-Run vs Short-Run Effects
description: A SaaS product team tests a new user onboarding checklist. After two weeks, the checklist shows a 15% increase in feature activation (features used in the first 30 days). The team ships. Six months later, retention for the onboarded cohort is 5% lower than historical rates. A retrospective analysis is conducted. Which experimental design flaw most plausibly explains the discrepancy?
options: The two-week test was statistically underpowered and the activation lift was a false positive

The test measured short-run activation but did not measure long-run retention — a feature that drives early engagement through friction (completing a checklist) may not create genuine long-term value, and the proxy metric of activation misled the team
The six-month retention data is confounded by external market changes, making comparison to historical rates invalid
The onboarding checklist should have been tested on a smaller cohort to reduce the impact of potential negative effects
explanation: This is a metric selection and experiment duration problem. The team chose a short-run proxy metric (feature activation) that was easy to measure quickly, but it did not reflect the true business goal (long-run retention). Onboarding checklists can inflate early activation by creating structured tasks that users complete but do not find intrinsically valuable — leading to higher feature usage in the first weeks but lower retention later because the engagement was compliance-driven rather than value-driven. The experimental fix is to either run the test long enough to observe retention directly, or to validate that the short-run metric predicts long-run outcomes. Option A (underpowered) is less likely — the 15% lift is large and would have been detectable at most reasonable sample sizes. Option C (external confounds) is possible but is a weaker explanation without evidence of market changes. Option D (smaller cohort) does not address the core issue of metric selection.
hints: Ask whether the metric you can measure in the test window is genuinely predictive of the metric you ultimately care about.
Consider whether a behavior change driven by the experiment's mechanism (a checklist) reflects durable user value.

title: Variance Reduction: Stratified Randomization
description: A marketplace is testing a new fee structure for sellers. Seller revenue is highly variable — some sellers earn $500/month, others earn $50,000/month. The team uses simple random assignment. A data scientist recommends stratified randomization by seller revenue tier instead. Why would stratified randomization help in this context?
options: Stratified randomization increases the sample size by duplicating observations within strata

By ensuring that high-revenue and low-revenue sellers are proportionally balanced between treatment and control, stratified randomization reduces the chance that one arm accidentally contains more top sellers — decreasing variance in the treatment effect estimate
Stratification is only useful when there are fewer than 1,000 participants, not for large marketplace experiments
Stratified randomization prevents novelty effects by ensuring user segments are equally exposed to the new fee structure
explanation: In a highly skewed distribution like seller revenue, simple random assignment can accidentally produce large imbalances — e.g., 60% of top-tier sellers ending up in treatment just by chance. These imbalances inflate variance in the estimated treatment effect. Stratified randomization blocks assignment within revenue tiers, guaranteeing that each stratum contributes proportionally to both arms. This reduces between-group variance attributable to the known covariate (revenue tier) and improves the precision of the estimate — equivalent in spirit to post-stratification adjustment but implemented at assignment time. Option A is wrong — stratification does not change sample size. Option C is a misconception — stratification is beneficial regardless of sample size, though its advantages are more apparent with smaller samples or highly skewed covariates. Option D confuses stratification with a completely different design consideration — it has no effect on novelty.
hints: Random assignment is unbiased on average, but in any single draw it can produce imbalances — stratification reduces how much those imbalances affect your estimate.
Think about what happens to your treatment effect estimate if all the highest-revenue sellers happen to land in one arm.

title: Guardrail Metrics and Ship Decisions
description: A consumer app tests a new ad format. The primary metric — ad click-through rate — improves by 22% (p=0.001). However, a guardrail metric — 7-day user retention — drops by 1.8% (p=0.02). The ad team argues the retention drop is small in absolute terms and wants to ship based on the strong primary metric lift. What is the most principled decision framework?
options: Ship — the primary metric is what matters and a 1.8% retention drop is within acceptable noise
Do not ship — any statistically significant deterioration in a guardrail metric should block shipping until the root cause is understood and the tradeoff is explicitly evaluated by stakeholders
Run the test longer to see if the retention drop recovers
Segment by user type to check if the retention drop is concentrated in low-value users who can be excluded
explanation: Guardrail metrics exist precisely to catch cases where optimizing a primary metric creates harmful side effects. A statistically significant 1.8% drop in 7-day retention is not noise — it signals that users exposed to the new ad format are churning at a higher rate. The responsible decision is to block shipping, investigate the mechanism (is the ad format intrusive? is it degrading the core experience?), and escalate the tradeoff to stakeholders who can make a business decision about whether the revenue from ad clicks outweighs the retention cost. Option A uses the primary metric to override a significant guardrail violation, which defeats the purpose of having guardrails. Running longer (option C) is unlikely to make the retention drop disappear if users genuinely dislike the experience. Segmenting to find 'acceptable' users to exclude (option D) is rationalizing the harm rather than addressing it.
hints: A guardrail metric that deteriorates significantly is a red flag, not a data point to explain away.
Ask what the purpose of guardrail metrics is — and what it means to override them.

title: Power Calculation: Effect of Increasing Variance
description: A data scientist is planning an A/B test to detect a 5% relative lift in daily revenue per user. The baseline daily revenue is $10 with a standard deviation of $8. At 80% power and α=0.05, the required sample size is 800 users per arm. The team discovers that a recent pricing change has pushed the standard deviation to $16 (revenue variance is now 4x higher). If everything else stays constant, what is the approximate required sample size per arm now?
options: Still approximately 800 — the mean and target effect size have not changed
Approximately 3,200 — sample size scales with the square of the standard deviation, so doubling the standard deviation quadruples the required sample size
Approximately 1,600 — sample size scales linearly with the standard deviation, so doubling the standard deviation doubles the required sample size
Approximately 400 — higher variance means more information per user, reducing the required sample size
explanation: The formula for required sample size in a two-sample test is proportional to σ²/δ², where σ is the standard deviation and δ is the effect size (in absolute terms). When σ doubles from $8 to $16, σ² quadruples, so the required sample size quadruples from 800 to approximately 3,200 per arm. This is one reason why high-variance metrics (like revenue) require much larger experiments than lower-variance metrics (like binary conversion rates). Option A is wrong — variance directly determines the precision of the estimate and a large increase in variance has a major impact on required sample size. Option C assumes linear scaling, which would be correct if sample size scaled with σ rather than σ². Option D has the relationship backwards — higher variance means more noise, requiring more data, not less.
hints: The required sample size formula involves the variance term squared — think about what happens when the standard deviation doubles.
Higher variance in the outcome metric means each additional observation gives you less precise information about the treatment effect.

title: Quasi-Experimental Method Selection
description: A fintech company wants to measure the impact of a regulatory change that forced it to add a friction step (identity verification) to its onboarding flow for users in the EU. The change was implemented on a fixed date and applies to all EU users — it was not randomized. The company has 18 months of pre-change data and 6 months of post-change data for both EU and non-EU users. Which analytical approach is most appropriate for estimating the causal effect of the friction step?
options: A simple pre-post comparison for EU users: compare average conversion before and after the change date
A difference-in-differences design using EU users as the treatment group and non-EU users as the control group, assuming parallel trends in the absence of the regulation
A random sample of EU users should be compared to a random sample of non-EU users post-change
The effect cannot be estimated because there is no control group in the EU
explanation: This is a classic quasi-experimental setup where a natural experiment (regulatory change) provides exogenous variation. A difference-in-differences design compares the change in outcomes for EU users (treatment) before and after the policy to the change in outcomes for non-EU users (control) over the same period. By using non-EU users as a concurrent comparison group, the design controls for time trends and other concurrent changes that would confound a simple pre-post analysis. The key identifying assumption — parallel trends — requires that EU and non-EU users would have followed similar trajectories absent the regulation, which the 18 months of pre-period data can be used to test. Option A (pre-post only) fails to account for any simultaneous changes in market conditions, seasonal patterns, or platform changes. Option C compares groups at a single point in time, ignoring the natural control provided by the non-EU group's trajectory. Option D is wrong — the non-EU group provides exactly the control group needed.
hints: When a policy applies to one group but not another at the same time, you can use the unaffected group as a comparison.
Think about what a simple before-after comparison misses that a concurrent comparison group would capture.

title: Multi-Armed Bandit vs A/B Test Trade-offs
description: A media company is testing four different content recommendation algorithms. An engineer proposes using a multi-armed bandit (MAB) approach rather than a traditional A/B test to 'automatically route traffic to the best algorithm.' The data scientist points out that a MAB approach has a specific trade-off the team should understand. What is the most important trade-off?
options: Multi-armed bandits are always inferior to A/B tests because they cannot handle more than two arms

A multi-armed bandit optimizes for short-run performance by exploiting the best-performing arm early, but this exploration-exploitation trade-off means the losing arms get less traffic — which reduces the statistical precision of estimates for those arms and makes it harder to definitively determine which algorithm is best
Multi-armed bandits require more total traffic than A/B tests to reach the same confidence level
Multi-armed bandits are only valid when all arms have the same baseline conversion rate
explanation: The fundamental trade-off of multi-armed bandits is between exploration (learning about all arms) and exploitation (directing traffic to the current best). As the MAB allocates more traffic to the leading arm, the trailing arms receive less data — making their estimates noisier and reducing the power to detect true differences between them. This is the right approach when the primary goal is to maximize cumulative reward during the experiment, but it compromises inferential quality. If the team needs to know definitively which algorithm is best (for long-run deployment decisions), a balanced A/B test is more appropriate. Option A is wrong — MABs handle multiple arms and are well-suited for that use case. Option B (requiring more traffic) is not generally true — MABs can be more efficient in cumulative reward terms, though less efficient for inferential precision. Option D is a misconception — MABs work regardless of baseline conversion rate differences.
hints: Multi-armed bandits are designed to minimize regret during the experiment — think about what that means for how traffic is distributed.
Ask whether the goal is to maximize performance during the test or to learn which option is definitively best.

title: Interaction Effects in Concurrent Experiments
description: A SaaS company runs two simultaneous A/B tests on the same users: one testing a new pricing page (Experiment P) and one testing a new email sequence (Experiment E). Both experiments use independent randomization. The pricing page test shows a significant 8% conversion lift. Six months later, an analyst discovers that users in the treatment arm of Experiment P were twice as likely to also be in the treatment arm of Experiment E due to a hash collision in the randomization code. What problem does this create?
options: The two experiments are still valid — independent randomization guarantees they cannot interact

The hash collision creates correlation between experiment assignments — users who saw both treatments simultaneously cannot be distinguished from users who only saw the pricing page treatment, making it impossible to cleanly attribute the 8% lift to the pricing page alone
This is only a problem if the email experiment also showed a significant result
The experiments should be combined into a single factorial design to measure the interaction effect
explanation: When two experiments are correlated due to a hash collision, the assignment in one experiment predicts the assignment in the other. In this case, users in pricing-page treatment were overrepresented in email-sequence treatment. This means the measured 'pricing page effect' is actually a mixture of the pricing page effect and the email sequence effect — or their interaction — because users in the treatment arm received both changes at elevated rates. The 8% lift cannot be attributed to the pricing page alone. Option A is wrong — independent randomization should guarantee independence, but the hash collision broke that guarantee. Option C is a common but incorrect intuition — even if only one experiment showed significance, the confounding still invalidates the individual attribution. Option D (factorial design) would be the right design choice going forward, but it does not fix the retrospective problem created by the collision.
hints: When two randomizations are correlated, receiving one treatment predicts receiving the other — they are no longer independent experiments.
Think about what it means for your effect estimate if treatment users were systematically more likely to also receive a second treatment.

title: FDR vs FWER: Choosing the Right Correction
description: A growth team at a consumer app runs a single experiment and simultaneously tests 50 secondary metrics at α=0.05. They find 8 significant results. The head of data asks the analyst to apply a multiple testing correction, and two options are on the table: a family-wise error rate (FWER) control approach vs. a false discovery rate (FDR) control approach. The team expects roughly 5 truly significant metrics out of the 50. Which correction approach is more appropriate for this use case, and why?
options: FWER control is more appropriate because it guarantees zero false positives among the discoveries

FDR control is more appropriate — when testing a large number of hypotheses where some true effects are expected, FDR control targets the proportion of false positives among discoveries, preserving more true positives while still bounding the error rate. FWER control would be overly conservative and discard too many real findings
Both approaches produce identical results when applied to the same dataset
FWER is more appropriate because it is easier to explain to non-technical stakeholders than FDR
explanation: FWER control (e.g., using a Bonferroni-type correction) bounds the probability of even one false positive. This is appropriate when any single false positive is unacceptable — for example, clinical trials or high-stakes regulatory decisions. However, with 50 hypotheses, FWER control divides alpha by 50, requiring p < 0.001 for significance, which is extremely conservative and will discard many true effects. When you expect several true effects and can tolerate some false discoveries as long as the overall false discovery rate is controlled (e.g., at 10%), FDR control methods are far more powerful. In this scenario with ~5 expected true effects, FDR control recovers most of them while FWER would suppress nearly all of them. Option A overstates FWER — it controls the probability of any false positive but does not guarantee zero. Option C is wrong — FDR and FWER corrections produce different rejection sets. Option D prioritizes communication over statistical appropriateness, which is backwards.
hints: Think about what each approach is controlling — one controls the probability of any error, the other controls the proportion of errors among significant findings.
In a large-scale test where some true effects are expected, consider which error rate is most meaningful to bound.
concepts: TYPE I AND TYPE II ERRORS

title: Multiple Testing Family Definition
description: A product analytics team at an e-commerce company runs experiments across four independent product areas: checkout, search, recommendations, and email. Each product area team runs two experiments per month. The head of data asks whether the teams should apply a family-wise multiple testing correction across all experiments company-wide. Which argument best captures the correct approach to defining the 'family' for multiple testing correction?
options: All experiments across the company should always be corrected together because they share the same database

The appropriate 'family' for correction is determined by the shared inferential context — experiments addressing independent business questions in separate product areas generally do not require cross-area correction, but metrics tested within a single experiment do. Correction should be applied within a test's metric family, not across unrelated tests
No correction is needed as long as each experiment uses p < 0.05 individually
All experiments in a calendar month should be corrected together regardless of product area
explanation: The concept of a 'family' in multiple testing refers to a set of hypotheses that share a common inferential context — where a false positive in any one of them would contribute to a misleading overall conclusion. Metrics tested within a single experiment to answer a single question (e.g., 'does this feature improve user experience?') form a natural family requiring correction. By contrast, an experiment on checkout and an experiment on email recommendations are answering completely different business questions for different teams — a false positive in one does not create a compounded error for the other. Applying company-wide correction would be overly conservative and suppress many valid findings. Option A applies correction too broadly — the shared database is irrelevant to statistical independence. Option C ignores the real multiple comparisons issue within experiments. Option D (monthly grouping) uses an arbitrary temporal boundary with no statistical justification.
hints: Ask what would be misleading if one test in the group were a false positive — if it only affects one team's isolated decision, it may not need to be in the same family as other tests.
The 'family' should group tests that share a common question, not tests that share a calendar period or database.

title: CUPED: When Pre-Experiment Data Does Not Help
description: A team at a social media platform wants to use pre-experiment engagement data as a covariate to reduce variance in a test of a new notification format. The lead data scientist warns that in this specific case, the variance reduction may be minimal. The experiment targets brand-new users who have zero pre-experiment history. What does this reveal about when covariate adjustment is most valuable?
options: Covariate adjustment is always valuable regardless of the correlation between the covariate and the outcome

Covariate adjustment provides variance reduction proportional to the squared correlation between the covariate and the outcome — if the covariate is zero or nearly zero for all users (new users have no history), the correlation is near zero and little variance is removed
New users should be excluded from all experiments because they lack historical data for proper analysis
The team should use demographic data instead of engagement data since new users always have demographics available
explanation: The variance reduction from covariate adjustment is equal to ρ²·Var(Y), where ρ is the correlation between the covariate and the outcome. When the covariate is pre-experiment behavior and all users in the experiment are brand new, their pre-experiment values are all zero — a constant, not a variable. A constant covariate has zero variance and therefore zero correlation with the outcome, meaning the covariate adjustment reduces variance by exactly 0%. This is a common misconception: teams apply variance reduction methods assuming they always help, without checking whether the covariate is actually predictive of the outcome in the specific experiment cohort. Option A is directly contradicted by the math. Option C is wrong — new users are often the most important cohort to study; they just require different variance reduction strategies (e.g., randomization-based methods). Option D may help if demographics are correlated with outcome, but this should be empirically verified, not assumed.
hints: The benefit of using a pre-experiment covariate depends entirely on how much it can predict the outcome — ask what happens when that predictive power is zero.
Think about what pre-experiment data looks like for users who have never used the product before.

title: Variance Reduction: Winsorization Trade-offs
description: A marketplace platform uses revenue per seller per week as its primary experiment metric. Revenue is highly skewed — the top 0.5% of sellers account for 30% of total revenue. The data science team debates between two variance reduction approaches: (A) winsorizing revenue at the 99th percentile, and (B) using a pre-experiment revenue covariate. The team needs to make a recommendation. Which consideration should drive the choice between the two approaches?
options: Winsorization is always preferred because it is simpler to implement and explain

The choice depends on the goal: winsorization changes the estimand by capping extreme values — the result represents average effect excluding top sellers — while covariate adjustment preserves the full estimand and reduces variance by explaining pre-existing differences. If top sellers are a target user segment, winsorization may produce misleading business conclusions
Covariate adjustment is always superior because winsorization introduces bias by removing data
Both approaches produce equivalent results when the covariate is revenue from the prior period
explanation: Winsorization and covariate adjustment are both valid variance reduction techniques but with different implications. Winsorization changes the metric itself — revenue capped at the 99th percentile estimates the average treatment effect excluding the top tail of sellers. If those sellers are precisely the segment the team cares about (they generate 30% of revenue), then the winsorized estimate is not answering the right question. Covariate adjustment, by contrast, does not modify the outcome — it uses pre-experiment revenue to explain variance in the observed outcome, reducing noise without changing the estimand. The right approach depends on whether the business wants the effect on all sellers or on the truncated distribution. Option A incorrectly prioritizes implementation simplicity over statistical correctness. Option C overstates the case for covariate adjustment — it is not always superior, especially when pre-experiment data has low predictive power (new users). Option D is wrong — the two methods will generally produce different estimates.
hints: When you cap extreme values, you are no longer estimating the effect on those extreme users — ask whether they matter for the business decision.
Covariate adjustment reduces noise around the original metric; winsorization changes the metric itself.

title: Cluster Randomization: Statistical Efficiency Loss
description: A food delivery app wants to test a new dispatch algorithm. Due to network effects between couriers and customers in the same geographic area, the team decides to randomize at the city level rather than the individual courier level. The platform operates in 40 cities, with 200–2,000 couriers per city. A statistician warns the team about the design efficiency implications. What is the primary statistical concern with city-level randomization?
options: City-level randomization increases statistical power because each city is a larger unit of observation

City-level randomization dramatically reduces the effective sample size — the number of independent units is now 40 cities, not thousands of couriers. High intra-cluster correlation means couriers within the same city behave similarly, so each additional courier adds little independent information
The design is invalid because cities are not randomly selected from a larger population
City-level randomization is only appropriate when all cities have the same number of couriers
explanation: The key concept here is the design effect (DEFF) in cluster randomization, driven by the intra-cluster correlation coefficient (ICC). If couriers within the same city tend to behave similarly (high ICC), then observing 2,000 couriers in one city provides far less information than observing 2,000 independent couriers spread across many cities. The effective sample size is approximately n / (1 + (m-1)·ICC), where m is the cluster size. With high ICC and large clusters, the effective sample size can collapse dramatically — 40 cities may provide the statistical power of a few hundred independent observations, not tens of thousands. Option A has the relationship backwards — city-level units are larger but they are fewer and less independent. Option C is wrong — cluster-randomized designs are valid even when clusters are not a probability sample; the randomization is across clusters. Option D is incorrect — unequal cluster sizes can be handled analytically.
hints: When users within a cluster behave similarly, each additional user in the cluster contributes less new information than an independent user would.
Think about the effective number of independent observations, not the raw count of individuals.

title: Network Effects: Two-Sided Market Measurement
description: An online marketplace tests a new buyer incentive (cashback for first purchase). The test randomizes individual buyers: 50% get the cashback offer, 50% do not. After four weeks, treatment buyers purchase 20% more than control. Leadership wants to estimate the platform-wide revenue impact of rolling out the cashback to all buyers. A researcher flags that the measured 20% should not be used directly. Why?
options: The 20% lift is a biased estimate because cashback incentives always create novelty effects

The individual-level test captures a partial equilibrium effect — when only 50% of buyers have the incentive, there is sufficient seller capacity for all of them. At full rollout, all buyers compete for the same seller inventory simultaneously, potentially creating supply constraints that reduce the per-buyer benefit below the measured 20%
The test should have been run on sellers, not buyers, to measure the true marketplace impact
The 20% lift overestimates the effect because control buyers are contaminated by seeing treatment buyers' cashback badges
explanation: This is the partial equilibrium vs. general equilibrium problem in marketplace experiments. In the A/B test, only 50% of buyers are incentivized, so sellers have ample capacity to fulfill treatment buyers' increased demand. The 20% per-buyer lift is a local, partial-equilibrium estimate. But when cashback rolls out to 100% of buyers, all buyers increase demand simultaneously — if seller supply is inelastic (e.g., there are only so many products or service slots), prices rise or availability falls, dampening the per-buyer benefit. The true platform-wide impact may be significantly lower than 20%. Option A attributes the issue to novelty, which is a different concern. Option C suggests redesigning the experiment — testing sellers might be appropriate for a seller incentive, but the researcher's concern is about scaling, not experimental unit selection. Option D (control contamination from seeing badges) could be a real concern in some designs but is not the main issue raised — the researcher is pointing to supply-demand equilibrium.
hints: In a two-sided market, what happens to supply when all buyers simultaneously increase demand?
A test where only some users receive a treatment may not replicate conditions that exist when all users receive it.

title: Heterogeneous Treatment Effects: Power-User Segment
description: A SaaS tool tests a new keyboard shortcut feature. Overall, the experiment shows a non-significant 1% increase in task completion rate (p=0.18). An analyst segments by usage frequency and finds that power users (top 20% by weekly sessions) show a significant 11% improvement (p=0.004), while casual users show a non-significant -0.5% change. The team considers shipping to power users only. What is the most rigorous interpretation of these findings?
