options: The power-user segment is confirmed to benefit — the significant p-value validates the effect and shipping to that segment is straightforward

The segment finding is promising but should be treated as hypothesis-generating, not confirmatory — the power-user segment was identified post-hoc from a failed overall test, creating multiple comparisons risk. A follow-up experiment pre-specified for power users would provide confirmatory evidence
Since casual users show a negative (though non-significant) trend, the feature should not be shipped to any segment
The overall null result overrides the segment finding — by definition, if the overall test is not significant, no subgroup can be significant
explanation: Post-hoc segmentation of a null overall result is a well-known source of spurious findings. The analyst tested at least two segments (power users and casual users) after observing that the overall test was not significant — this is multiple comparisons in action, and p=0.004 in the power-user segment might be a false positive. The correct treatment is to use this finding to design a targeted follow-up experiment with power users as the pre-specified population and power-user task completion as the pre-registered primary metric. This follow-up would be confirmatory, not exploratory. Option A commits the post-hoc segmentation error by treating the p-value as directly valid without accounting for the exploratory analysis path taken to find it. Option C uses the non-significant negative finding for casual users to override a plausible positive segment — non-significance is not evidence of no effect. Option D is a common misconception; overall null results do not mathematically prevent segment-level significance, they just make it suspect without appropriate correction.
hints: When you divide data into segments after observing the overall result, you are implicitly running multiple tests — each segment is another opportunity for a false positive.
A significant post-hoc subgroup finding from a null overall test calls for replication in a targeted experiment, not immediate action.

title: Simpson's Paradox in Experiment Readout
description: A fintech app runs an A/B test on a new loan application flow. Overall conversion rate: control 14.2%, treatment 13.8% — treatment is lower (p=0.03). But when segmented by credit score tier: high credit (>700): treatment 18.1% vs control 16.4%; low credit (<700): treatment 9.2% vs control 8.8%. Treatment outperforms in both segments yet underperforms overall. The data team is confused. What explains this apparent paradox?
options: The segment-level analysis has a lower statistical power and the findings are likely noise

Simpson's paradox: treatment was disproportionately assigned to the low-credit segment (which has lower base conversion rates), making the overall treatment conversion appear worse even though treatment outperforms control within each credit tier
The p-value of 0.03 confirms the overall result is definitive — segment analysis should be ignored
This indicates a sample ratio mismatch — the randomization must have failed
explanation: This is a textbook instance of Simpson's paradox in experimentation. Even with correct randomization, if the segments are not balanced proportionally between treatment and control (e.g., more low-credit users ended up in treatment), the segment with the lower baseline conversion rate (low credit) drags down the overall treatment average more than the control average. Treatment outperforms in both segments individually, yet appears to underperform in the aggregate. The resolution is to analyze the weighted average of segment-level effects or to verify whether the segment distribution is truly balanced. This can also indicate an issue with the randomization if the imbalance is large. Option A dismisses the segment findings, but the analysis is valid — the confusion lies in aggregation, not power. Option C uses the overall p-value to dismiss segmentation, which is incorrect when there is a structural reason (composition imbalance) explaining the discrepancy. Option D (sample ratio mismatch) is a plausible concern but SRM refers to overall arm size, not segment composition within arms.
hints: When a treatment appears to underperform overall but outperforms in every subgroup, ask whether the groups have different compositions in treatment and control.
A subgroup that has a lower base rate being overrepresented in one arm can drag down that arm's overall average.

title: Early Stopping and Minimum Detectable Effect
description: A consumer app team pre-registers an A/B test for 28 days with a minimum detectable effect (MDE) of 5% at 80% power. After 10 days, a stakeholder notices the effect point estimate is already at 7.2% and pushes to stop early. The data scientist resists, noting that the confidence interval at day 10 is [-1.1%, 15.5%]. What does this interval reveal about the decision to stop?
options: The positive point estimate of 7.2% is above the MDE, so stopping early is statistically valid

The wide confidence interval spanning zero at day 10 shows that the test lacks sufficient precision to support a confident conclusion — the estimate is noisy and the true effect could plausibly be near zero or negative. Stopping early based on the point estimate risks acting on noise
The confidence interval is irrelevant — only the p-value matters for the stop decision
A 10-day interim result is always valid as long as the point estimate exceeds the pre-registered MDE
explanation: The confidence interval at day 10 — [-1.1%, 15.5%] — is wide enough to include zero and even slightly negative effects. This tells us the estimate is not yet precise enough to distinguish a genuine 7% lift from random noise. The point estimate of 7.2% is compatible with the observed data but so is an effect near zero. The MDE is a planning concept: it is the smallest effect the test can detect at the planned sample size with 80% power. Stopping at 10 days means you have far fewer observations than planned, reducing precision. Option A confuses the MDE (a planning threshold) with the precision of the current estimate — they are different things. Option C dismisses the confidence interval, which is one of the most informative outputs of the analysis. Option D restates option A's error — exceeding the MDE at 10 days is not sufficient for early stopping because the estimate is too noisy at that stage.
hints: A point estimate tells you the most likely value, but the confidence interval tells you how uncertain you are — look at whether the interval rules out a null effect.
The MDE was computed for the full planned sample size — it does not apply to interim looks at partial samples.

title: Duration: Lifecycle-Dependent Metrics
description: A B2B SaaS company tests a new in-product analytics dashboard for enterprise customers. The primary metric is 'report exports per user per month.' The team plans a 14-day test, reasoning that two weeks captures enough usage to measure the effect. A customer success manager pushes back, noting that enterprise workflows are monthly. What is the most valid concern about the 14-day test window for this metric?
options: A 14-day test is too long — enterprise users adopt new features slowly and two weeks would already show full adoption

Report exports are tied to end-of-month reporting cycles — a 14-day window will capture partial cycles and may not include the month-end activity that drives most report usage, leading to an underestimate of the feature's impact on a per-month basis
The metric is a ratio (per user per month) and cannot be measured accurately in a sub-monthly window
Enterprise customers should be excluded from A/B tests because their contracts require feature parity
explanation: When a metric is inherently tied to a periodic business cycle, tests that do not cover at least one full cycle will produce incomplete measurements. Enterprise report exports are driven by financial close, board reporting, and monthly review cycles — the majority of exports may happen in the last few days of each month. A 14-day window that starts mid-month may capture very few high-volume export events and underestimate the feature's impact, or it may accidentally start near month-end, overestimating impact. The experiment duration should be at least 30 days (preferably 60 to capture two cycles for stability) to measure the metric that the team actually cares about. Option A is wrong — the concern is the opposite of too long. Option C is incorrect — ratios can be estimated from sub-monthly windows; the issue is not mathematical but about whether the window captures representative behavior. Option D is a business concern, not a statistical one, and does not address the measurement question.
hints: Ask whether the behavior you are trying to measure is evenly distributed over time or clustered around specific calendar events.
A test window should cover at least one complete natural cycle of the metric's main driver.

title: Minimum Detectable Effect and Business Viability
description: A streaming platform wants to test whether showing a 'continue watching' row at the top of the home screen increases subscription renewals. The renewal rate is currently 78%, and the business case requires detecting a 0.5 percentage point improvement (to 78.5%) to justify the engineering cost. A power calculation shows that detecting a 0.5pp lift at 80% power and α=0.05 requires 420,000 users per arm. The platform has 300,000 monthly active users. How should the team respond?
options: Run the test anyway — 300,000 users per arm is close enough to detect a 0.5pp lift

The test is fundamentally underpowered at current traffic levels for the required MDE. Options include accepting a larger MDE (e.g., 1pp), accumulating users over multiple months, accepting lower power, or making the ship decision without a controlled experiment given the traffic constraint
Lower the alpha to 0.01 to compensate for the lower sample size
The platform should recruit new users to the test to reach the required sample size
explanation: This is a traffic-constraint problem: the required sample size (420,000 per arm = 840,000 total) exceeds the entire monthly active user base (300,000). There is no way to run this test at the required power within a single month. The team has several honest options: relax the MDE to a larger effect that is detectable with 150,000 per arm, run for multiple months to accumulate the required sample, explicitly accept lower power (knowing they will miss the effect most of the time even if it exists), or make a judgment call without a rigorous experiment. Option A is wrong — 300,000 is not per arm but total; even if it were per arm, a 30% shortfall from 420,000 meaningfully reduces power. Lowering alpha (option C) reduces the false positive rate but also reduces power — it makes the situation worse, not better. Recruiting new users (option D) changes the target population and would measure an effect for a different user cohort than the one the business cares about.
hints: When required sample size exceeds available traffic, there is no way to reach the planned power without changing the design parameters.
Consider what options exist when the experiment simply cannot be run as designed — the answer is rarely 'run it anyway.'

title: Heterogeneous Effects: When to Segment Pre-Registration
description: A mobile gaming company is launching a new difficulty calibration system. Before running the experiment, a game designer predicts that new players (< 7 days in app) will benefit most because the system addresses early churn, while veteran players (> 90 days) may react negatively because they have already formed habits. A data scientist must decide whether to make this segmentation part of the pre-registered analysis plan. What is the best approach?
options: Never pre-register segment analyses — they should always be exploratory to preserve flexibility

Pre-register the primary metric at the overall level and also pre-register the new-player and veteran segments as pre-specified subgroup analyses with appropriately adjusted alpha levels — this provides confirmatory power for the hypothesized segment effects while acknowledging the additional comparisons
Run the overall test first, and if it is null, then look at segments to find where the effect might be hiding
Segment results are only valid if the segments are of equal size, so the analysis should use a balanced sample
explanation: Pre-registering segment analyses when there is a strong a priori hypothesis — grounded in product logic and user behavior theory — is the correct scientific approach. By committing to the segments and their expected directions before seeing the data, the team preserves the confirmatory nature of the analysis and can apply appropriate alpha adjustments (e.g., testing at α=0.025 per segment to maintain an overall 5% error rate). This is superior to purely exploratory post-hoc segmentation, which inflates false positive risk, and it is also superior to option A's blanket prohibition on pre-registered segments. Option A loses the ability to make confirmatory claims about important subgroups. Option C is the post-hoc exploration pattern that risks false discoveries — using segment analysis to 'rescue' a null overall result is exactly the wrong way to use subgroup analysis. Option D is incorrect — pre-specified segment analyses do not require equal segment sizes; statistical tests account for different sample sizes.
hints: There is an important distinction between pre-specifying a segment analysis based on prior knowledge and diving into segments only after the overall test disappoints.
When a hypothesis about segment differences is grounded in strong product intuition before the experiment, it can be part of the registered analysis plan.

title: CUPED Covariate Window: Contamination Through Post-Exposure Measurement
code_snippet:
# CUPED adjustment for a 14-day checkout rate A/B test
# Intended: Y_cuped = Y - theta * (X - E[X])
# X should be a pre-experiment covariate

experiment_data = load_experiment_data()
# Fields: user_id, treatment (0/1),
#   Y = checkout rate during experiment days 1–14
#   X = checkout rate during experiment days 1–14  ← same window as Y

theta = np.cov(Y, X)[0, 1] / np.var(X)
Y_cuped = Y - theta * (X - np.mean(X))

report = {
    'variance_reduction': '68%',   # unusually high
    'p_value': 0.021,
    'estimated_lift': '+0.3%'      # suspiciously small vs prior tests
}
description: The analyst applies CUPED and reports 68% variance reduction and a statistically significant but tiny +0.3% lift. Prior tests on comparable features showed 1–2% lifts. What is the root cause of this suspicious result?
options: X is measured during the same experiment window as Y, so treatment group users' X values are influenced by the treatment itself; the contaminated covariate inflates theta and causes the CUPED adjustment to over-correct treatment group outcomes toward the control mean — the lift is underestimated and the variance reduction is overstated; X must be computed from a pre-experiment window (e.g., checkout rate during the 14 days before day 0) when it cannot be affected by treatment assignment

68% variance reduction is correct and desirable — high variance reduction confirms CUPED is working well; the +0.3% lift is likely the true effect, and prior tests showing 1–2% lifts should be re-examined for methodology errors rather than assuming the current result is wrong

The variance reduction formula has a sign error: Y_cuped should add the adjustment term (Y + theta * (X − E[X])) rather than subtract it; the subtraction artificially deflates treatment group adjusted outcomes, making the lift appear smaller than the true effect

Using the same metric for both Y and X creates circular adjustment regardless of time window — CUPED requires the covariate to be a different metric from the outcome variable; the fix is to use a proxy metric such as page views or session count as X instead of checkout rate
explanation:
Option A is correct. CUPED removes pre-existing variance attributable to baseline user behavior — improving sensitivity without biasing the causal estimate — but only if the covariate X is measured in a period unaffected by treatment assignment. When X is measured during the experiment window, treatment group users' X values co-move with Y under the treatment effect. This inflates cov(Y, X), which inflates theta. The adjustment Y_cuped = Y − theta*(X − E[X]) then over-corrects treatment group outcomes toward the control mean, producing an underestimated lift and an overstated variance reduction. The 68% variance reduction and near-zero lift are the dual signature of this contamination. Fix: compute X from the 14 days before experiment start — the same metric, but measured when no treatment has been applied.

Option B is wrong: while high variance reduction is desirable in principle, it should be interpreted in context. When combined with a lift that contradicts prior evidence from similar tests, it warrants investigation. Accepting the result without auditing the covariate window is a methodological error.

Option C is wrong: the CUPED formula is correctly written as Y minus the adjustment term. Adding the adjustment would introduce bias in the opposite direction. The sign is not the bug.

Option D is a misconception. Using the same metric measured in a pre-experiment window as the covariate is the standard and most effective CUPED formulation — pre-period checkout rate typically has the highest correlation with in-experiment checkout rate among all candidate covariates. The bug is the time window, not the choice of metric.
hints: The covariate X is measured during the same 14-day window as the experiment. For users in the treatment group, is their checkout rate during this window guaranteed to be unaffected by the treatment assignment?

When X co-moves with Y under treatment, the estimated theta is inflated relative to a pre-experiment covariate. An over-inflated theta over-corrects the treatment group's outcomes — does this make the estimated lift larger or smaller than the true effect?

title: Two-Sided Marketplace Equilibration: Why Short-Duration Tests Miss Steady-State Effects
scenario_context: A marketplace platform tests a new seller pricing tool that makes it easier to set competitive prices. The experiment runs 14 days with 50,000 sellers per arm. At day 14, the primary metric — GMV per buyer visit — shows no significant effect (p = 0.31, estimated lift +0.2%). The team marks the experiment as failed. Six weeks later, a holdout group analysis reveals +4.3% GMV in the treatment group versus the holdout.
description: Why did the 14-day read produce a null result while the six-week holdout revealed a meaningful positive effect?
options: Two-sided marketplace interventions require an equilibration period: sellers must discover and experiment with the pricing tool over days to weeks, and buyers must discover and respond to the resulting price competition over additional weeks — the full steady-state effect only emerges after both sides have adapted; at day 14, early seller adoption was incomplete and buyer behavioral response had barely begun, making the GMV lift near zero at that horizon

The experiment was underpowered at 14 days: with 50,000 sellers per arm the minimum detectable effect was larger than 4.3%, so the 14-day read was always statistically unable to detect the true effect; running the same experiment for 14 days with a larger sample would have shown significance

The six-week holdout is confounded by network spillovers: holdout buyers who interacted with treated sellers received partial treatment through price competition, inflating the apparent treatment-vs-holdout gap; the true incremental lift from the tool is smaller than 4.3% once spillover is corrected

The null result at day 14 reflects over-aggressive initial pricing: sellers first set prices too high using the new tool, suppressing buyer demand; by week 6 they had settled on rational prices, producing the observed lift; the 14-day read captured a temporary pricing overshoot rather than a stable effect
explanation:
Option A is correct. Two-sided marketplace interventions create a causal chain that spans both market sides. Sellers must (1) discover the tool, (2) run pricing experiments, and (3) arrive at competitive price points — a process that typically takes days to weeks. Buyers must then (4) encounter the changed prices in search results and (5) update their purchase behavior. At day 14, most sellers have only begun adoption and the downstream buyer behavioral shift is nascent. The GMV metric at day 14 measures an early-equilibration state rather than the eventual steady state. This is not a statistical power problem — the metric genuinely hadn't moved yet. Experiments that intervene on one side of a two-sided market need a duration that spans both sides' adaptation periods.

Option B misdiagnoses the problem. A standard power calculation with 50,000 sellers per arm and a 4.3% GMV lift would show high power at day 14. The null result is not caused by insufficient sample size — the metric itself was near zero because the causal chain hadn't completed. Extending duration (not sample size) would have detected the effect.

Option C inverts the contamination direction. If holdout buyers interacted with treated sellers, the holdout group's GMV would be contaminated upward, making the treatment-vs-holdout gap an underestimate of the true lift — not an overestimate. The contamination argument, if anything, makes the 4.3% figure conservative.

Option D is inconsistent with the data trajectory. An over-aggressive pricing scenario predicts treatment GMV below control initially, then convergence — not a path from near-zero gap at day 14 to +4.3% at six weeks. The observed trajectory matches gradual equilibration rather than correction of an overshoot.
hints: The intervention is on the seller side, but the primary metric reflects buyer purchase behavior. How many sequential behavioral steps separate a seller adopting the pricing tool from a buyer completing a purchase at the new price point?

If sellers need 2–3 weeks to fully adopt the tool and buyers need another 2–3 weeks to discover and respond to the resulting price changes, when would you expect to first observe a meaningful GMV lift?

title: High-variance revenue metric can't detect a real 2% lift — what's the structural diagnosis?
scenario_context: Your team runs an A/B test on a checkout upsell feature. The primary metric is revenue per session. After 14 days with 80K users per arm, the lift is +1.9% (p = 0.18, 95% CI: −0.9% to +4.7%). Your power analysis before launch showed 80% power to detect a 2% lift at α = 0.05. Post-hoc, you discover the metric's standard deviation is 3.8× higher than the estimate used in your pre-experiment power calc, driven by a small fraction of very high-spend sessions.
description: What is the root structural problem, and what is the right course of action?
options: The experiment ran for too short a time — extend to 28 days to double the sample and narrow the CI to significance.

Revenue per session is a low-sensitivity metric for this treatment: extreme high-spend sessions dominate variance, burying the effect even if it's real. Run a complementary analysis on a tighter metric (e.g., conversion rate) and pre-commit to a sensitivity-adjusted metric definition for the next experiment.
The pre-experiment power calc was wrong — redo it with the observed σ and rerun the experiment at the corrected sample size.
The lift is real but marginally underpowered; apply CUPED using pre-experiment revenue to recover the 20% variance reduction and push to significance.
explanation: The root problem is metric sensitivity: revenue per session has fat-tailed variance that makes it structurally under-powered for moderate-effect-size treatments. Adding more time (Option 0) gives more data but doesn't change the fundamental signal-to-noise ratio — if the metric variance is 3.8× the pre-calc estimate, you'd need ~14× more data to hit the original power, which is operationally infeasible. Re-doing the calc and rerunning (Option 2) is the right long-term fix but ignores the data already collected on conversion rate, which directly measures the treatment's intended effect and has far lower variance. CUPED (Option 3) helps but a 20% variance reduction against a 3.8× underestimate means you'd still be ~13× underpowered — CUPED doesn't rescue a fundamentally wrong metric choice. The correct action is to run a sensitivity diagnosis: which metric definition is tight enough to be detectable at this sample, what does conversion rate show (it's a legitimate guardrail), and re-anchor the primary metric for future experiments on this feature.
hints: If the observed σ was 3.8× the estimate used in the power calc, by roughly how much does the required sample size change?
Metric sensitivity is about which metrics are structurally detectable at your operational sample size. What property of revenue per session makes it low-sensitivity here?

title: Stakeholder writes the null hypothesis after seeing early results — what's the problem?
scenario_context: A PM runs a checkout redesign experiment. On day 3 the PM sees conversion trending up +2% and writes the experiment brief: 'H0: conversion rate is unchanged. H1: conversion rate increases.' The experiment runs to completion (14 days). Final result: +1.8% lift, p = 0.03. The PM declares success and prepares to ship.
description: What is the critical validity problem with this analysis?
options: The hypothesis is one-tailed (directional). One-tailed tests require half the sample of two-tailed tests, so the reported p-value is artificially conservative and the real p-value is about 0.015.

The hypothesis was written after observing early trending data, which is post-hoc hypothesis specification (HARKing). The chosen directional H1 was informed by the early data peek, inflating Type I error beyond the nominal α regardless of the final p-value.
The hypothesis is stated incorrectly — H0 should specify an effect size (e.g., 'conversion rate increases by at least 1%'), not just 'unchanged'.
14 days is too short for a checkout experiment; the p = 0.03 result is likely driven by novelty effect rather than a durable improvement.
explanation: HARKing (Hypothesizing After Results are Known) invalidates the frequentist p-value guarantee. The PM observed a positive trend on day 3 and then specified a directional (one-tailed) H1 that matched the observation. This is equivalent to running a two-tailed test but only reporting the significant tail — it approximately halves the p-value without the statistical legitimacy of a pre-registered one-tailed test. The final p = 0.03 cannot be trusted because the probability of falsely rejecting H0 is no longer bounded at α = 0.05. Option A is backwards: a one-tailed test is more liberal, not more conservative — it would make the result easier to call significant, not harder. Option C misunderstands frequentist null hypothesis structure — H0 is always a point null ('no effect'), not a range; effect size enters via MDE in the power calculation, not the hypothesis. Option D raises a legitimate concern about novelty effects, but it is a separate issue from the primary problem (the invalidated hypothesis), and it does not explain the p-value inflation.
hints: If you see data trending positive and then write a directional hypothesis, how does that change the probability of seeing p < 0.05 under a true null?
What is the difference between a pre-registered one-tailed test and a one-tailed test written after seeing the data direction?
concepts: TYPE I AND TYPE II ERRORS

title: PM wants to test 'better engagement' — what must you establish before writing the hypothesis?
scenario_context: A product manager asks you to run an experiment on a new social feed algorithm. The stated goal is 'better engagement.' There is no experiment brief yet. You have 14 days of runway and 200K DAU. The PM expects a ship/no-ship decision at the end.
description: What is the minimum set of things you must establish before the hypothesis can be written?
options: Write H0: 'engagement is unchanged' and H1: 'engagement increases.' Run the experiment and compute significance on the most-moved metric at the end.

Agree on a single operationalised OEC (e.g., 7-day retained sessions per user, or daily active interactions), specify the guardrail metrics (e.g., user report rate, content quality score), and confirm the MDE that would justify a ship decision — only then write the hypothesis.
Run the experiment first with all available engagement metrics, identify which one shows the largest lift, and pre-register that metric retroactively as the primary OEC.
Ask the PM to define engagement, accept whatever definition they give, and run a t-test on that metric. The hypothesis follows mechanically from the metric.
explanation: A well-formed hypothesis requires three things before you can run: (1) a single operationalised primary metric (the OEC), agreed before exposure — 'engagement' is not a metric, it's a goal; (2) guardrail metrics that gate the ship decision (e.g., you could improve session count while degrading content quality); (3) a minimum detectable effect that the experiment is actually powered to find at your sample size. Without these, you cannot write a valid H0/H1 pair — you end up running a test with an undefined outcome. Option A is the textbook anti-pattern: writing an underdetermined hypothesis and mining the metric that moves most. Option C describes HARKing — choosing the primary metric retroactively after seeing results invalidates the p-value. Option D partially works (specifying a metric) but skips guardrails and MDE, which means you can't assess whether the experiment is actually powered to detect a meaningful effect and can't define what 'ship' means quantitatively.
hints: If 'engagement' maps to 5 different metrics, and you look at all 5 at the end and pick the one that moved, what happens to your false-positive rate?
What is the difference between a hypothesis you can reject and a question you can explore?

title: The experiment brief has the null and alternative backwards — find the flaw
scenario_context: An experiment brief reads: 'H0: The new checkout flow increases conversion rate. H1: The new checkout flow has no effect on conversion rate.' The team runs the experiment for 14 days. Result: p = 0.12. They conclude 'H1 is confirmed — the feature has no effect' and archive the experiment as a null result.
description: What is the fundamental error in this analysis?
options: The p-value of 0.12 should be compared against α = 0.1 instead of α = 0.05 for a null-result conclusion; the team used the wrong threshold.

The hypotheses are inverted. In null hypothesis testing, H0 is always the no-effect statement and H1 is the alternative (effect exists). A failure to reject H0 (p = 0.12) does not confirm H0 — it means the data are insufficient to rule it out. The team cannot claim 'no effect' from a non-significant result.
The null hypothesis must always specify a direction (e.g., 'conversion rate does not increase'). The brief is flawed because a directional H0 requires a one-tailed test.
p = 0.12 is actually borderline significant under Bayesian criteria; the team should compute a Bayes factor to confirm the null result before archiving.
explanation: The hypotheses are structurally reversed. In frequentist hypothesis testing, H0 is always the null (no-effect, status quo) statement and H1 is the alternative that you are trying to find evidence for. The brief swapped them: it set H0 as 'the feature works' and H1 as 'no effect.' This is not a legal structure for NHST — and the conclusion 'H1 is confirmed' compounds the error. Even if the hypotheses were correctly stated, p = 0.12 would only mean 'fail to reject H0,' not 'H0 is true.' Failing to reject a correctly-stated null does not prove the null. The team has confused statistical significance absence with evidence of absence — an error separate from the hypothesis inversion. Option A misidentifies the problem as a threshold choice, which doesn't address the structural inversion. Option C adds a directionality requirement that doesn't apply — one-tailed tests apply when you pre-register a direction, not when H0 is stated with 'does not increase.' Option D introduces Bayesian machinery that is irrelevant to fixing the foundational NHST structural error.
hints: In null hypothesis testing, what role does H0 always play — and what role does H1 always play?
Even if the hypotheses were correctly stated, what does p = 0.12 actually allow you to conclude about H0?

title: Experiment randomizes on 'users who click the new feature' — what's wrong with the unit of analysis?
scenario_context: A team tests a new onboarding tooltip. Their experiment design document states: 'Randomization unit: users who click the tooltip.' Treatment users see the full onboarding flow; control users see a brief dismissal message. After 10 days, treatment shows +12% activation rate (p = 0.001).
description: What is the critical flaw in this experiment design?
options: The experiment should randomize on sessions, not users, since a single user can click the tooltip multiple times and inflate the treatment group count.

Randomizing on 'users who click the tooltip' creates survivorship bias: only users who engaged with the new feature are in the experiment. This selects for highly motivated users, making the treatment and control groups non-comparable and biasing the activation lift estimate upward.
The 10-day duration is too short for activation experiments; the novelty of the tooltip itself likely drives the +12% lift regardless of the onboarding content.
Treatment and control should have been identical in appearance; showing a 'brief dismissal message' to control users changes their experience and contaminates the control arm.
explanation: The randomization unit is post-exposure to the new feature — only users who already clicked the tooltip are included. This is a textbook survivorship bias / self-selection bias: tooltip-clickers are not a random sample of users; they are the most curious, most engaged, or most confused segment. Any comparison between treatment and control within this selected group is measuring the effect on high-engagement users, not the effect of the tooltip on users in general. The +12% lift likely reflects the pre-existing motivation of clickers, not the tooltip's causal effect. The correct randomization: assign users to treatment/control before exposure, then measure activation across both groups regardless of whether they click the tooltip. Option A confuses the repeated-click observation issue with the sampling bias — session-level randomization has different tradeoffs but doesn't fix the selection problem. Option C raises novelty effects, which are a legitimate concern but secondary to the structural selection bias. Option D is partially valid (the control arm experience should be comparable) but is not the 'critical flaw' — the fundamental problem is that the sample is selected on future outcome-related behavior.
hints: Who gets into the experiment under this design — all users, or only users who already interacted with the new element?
If clicking the tooltip correlates with high intrinsic motivation to complete onboarding, what does the comparison measure?

title: Engineer re-randomizes users daily during a 14-day experiment — what goes wrong?
scenario_context: A team runs a 14-day A/B test on a homepage recommendation algorithm. An engineer discovers that the assignment service was re-randomizing users daily: each day, each user had a 50/50 chance of being in control or treatment independently. After 14 days, 30% of users saw both arms at different times. The analysis uses each user's last-day assignment to define their group.
description: What validity problem does the daily re-randomization introduce, and which metric is most affected?
options: Daily re-randomization increases statistical power because more users cycle through the treatment arm, giving more exposure data for the analysis.

Daily re-randomization causes treatment contamination: users who were in control on early days but treatment on later days — or vice versa — carry behavioral spillover between arms. The last-day assignment groups are not comparable because assignment history differs systematically. Long-latency metrics (e.g., 7-day retention) are most affected.
The only issue is that the sample size calculation assumed a fixed group size; re-randomization changes the effective n per arm and the standard error calculation is wrong.
Daily re-randomization is equivalent to a crossover design, which is more efficient; the analysis should use a paired t-test instead of an independent-samples test.
explanation: Stable unit treatment value assumption (SUTVA) requires that each unit is exposed to exactly one treatment throughout the experiment. Daily re-randomization violates this: users accumulate mixed treatment histories, and their behavior reflects a mixture of both arms. The last-day assignment as a group definition is particularly misleading — a user assigned to 'control' on day 14 may have experienced 7 days of treatment, making them systematically different from users who were in control the entire time. Long-latency metrics (7-day retention, repurchase rate) are the most affected because they integrate behavioral signals over days when the user's actual assignment was different from their classification. Option A is wrong: re-randomization does not increase power for within-user effects — it introduces variance from the mixed treatment history. Option C partially identifies a real issue (the n calculation is off) but misses the contamination, which is the more fundamental problem. Option D is wrong: a proper crossover design has carefully controlled treatment sequences, washout periods, and analyses the within-user treatment effect — daily coin-flip re-randomization does none of these.
hints: If a user is in treatment for 7 days and control for 7 days, which group does their behavior actually reflect?
What behavioral signals require multiple days to accumulate, and how are those signals corrupted when a user's assignment changes mid-experiment?

title: Carryover from prior experiment contaminates the control arm — assess the bias
scenario_context: Your team runs a pricing experiment (Experiment B) immediately after Experiment A ended. Experiment A tested a 10% discount for treatment users; it ended 3 days ago. Experiment B randomizes all users 50/50 into control (current price) and treatment (new payment UI). Analysis reveals that former Experiment A treatment users — who got the discount — are now 40% more likely to land in Experiment B's control arm due to a segmentation overlap in the assignment logic.
description: What is the direction and likely magnitude of bias in Experiment B's results?
options: No bias — the discount from Experiment A has ended and its effects should have dissipated in 3 days; Experiment B's control arm is unaffected.

Experiment B's control arm is enriched with users who received a recent discount (trained to expect lower prices). These users may purchase more in the short run (satisfying discount-trained behavior) or churn faster (disappointed by returned pricing). The control arm is not comparable to a fresh random sample; lift estimates on conversion or revenue are biased in an unknown direction.
Experiment B's treatment arm is contaminated, not the control arm; the segmentation overlap only affects the treatment group.
The bias is always upward: control users who received a prior discount have higher baseline conversion, making the treatment effect look smaller than it actually is.
explanation: The direction of bias is indeterminate without knowing the persistence of the discount's behavioral effect. Discount-conditioned users in the control arm may behave differently from fresh users in at least two ways: (1) they have elevated near-term purchase intent due to discount training (upward bias on control conversion, underestimating treatment lift), or (2) they are disappointed by the returned full price and churn faster (downward bias on control retention, overestimating treatment lift). Either way, the groups are not comparable because the control arm systematically overrepresents users with a specific and recent behavioral history. The bias direction is unknown from the experimental design alone — which means the lift estimate is unreliable regardless of direction. Option A is wrong: 3 days is insufficient for behavioral carryover to dissipate for price-sensitive users; purchase intent and expectation calibration can persist for weeks. Option C misidentifies which arm has the problem — the assignment overlap overrepresents prior-treatment users in the current control arm. Option D states a specific direction without justification; both directions are plausible.
hints: If control users were recently trained to expect lower prices, how might their baseline conversion compare to a fresh random sample?
Does behavioral carryover necessarily bias results in one direction, or can it go either way depending on what the prior treatment was?
concepts: TYPE I AND TYPE II ERRORS

title: Session-level randomization when users have multiple sessions — predict the bias
scenario_context: An e-commerce team randomizes at the session level for a checkout UI test: each session independently gets a 50/50 chance of seeing the new or old UI. Users average 3.2 sessions over the 14-day experiment. A heavy-use segment (top 20% of users by sessions, averaging 9.1 sessions) contributes 55% of total sessions. The primary metric is conversion rate per session.
description: Predict the primary validity problem with session-level randomization in this setup.
options: Session-level randomization is valid; each session is an independent observation and the conversion rate per session is a correct denominator. No bias is introduced.

Heavy users who have many sessions are more likely to experience both arms within the experiment period. Their sessions contribute cross-contamination: the same user's behavior in the control condition is influenced by prior treatment exposure (and vice versa), violating the independence assumption and biasing the treatment effect estimate toward zero.
The bias is that high-frequency users skew the session count but not the metric — since conversion rate is computed per session, the heavy-user concentration doesn't affect validity.
The bias direction is upward: heavy users convert at higher rates, and since they dominate the session count, they inflate both arms' conversion rates, making the lift estimate appear larger.
explanation: Session-level randomization violates the stable unit treatment value assumption (SUTVA) when users have multiple sessions. A user who sees treatment in session 1 carries behavioral exposure into their control session 2 — they've already seen the new UI, formed an opinion, potentially modified their cart state or intent. The same applies in reverse. This within-user cross-arm contamination is worst for heavy users (9.1 sessions avg), who contribute 55% of all sessions and are nearly certain to experience both arms. The treatment effect estimate is biased toward zero (attenuation bias) because control sessions of treatment-exposed users behave more like treatment than a pure control. This is why user-level randomization is the default: it ensures SUTVA holds at the unit of analysis that accumulates experience. Option A is incorrect — independence at the session level fails when the same user can appear in both arms. Option C makes the error of thinking that per-session normalization neutralizes the contamination — the metric denominator is correct but the contamination affects numerator behavior. Option D describes a different confound (heavy-user baseline conversion rate) that isn't the primary validity problem here.
hints: If a user sees the treatment UI in session 1 and then is assigned to control in session 2, what does their control session actually measure?
What does SUTVA require about the relationship between a unit's treatment assignment and its potential outcomes?

title: Predict whether p = 0.03 on a proxy is sufficient to ship when the OEC shows no effect
scenario_context: A content team runs a 14-day experiment testing algorithmic versus editorial curation. Pre-registered: OEC = 7-day content completion rate. Guardrails: session duration (min +0%), ad revenue (min -2%). Results at experiment end: OEC = +0.2% (p = 0.74), session duration = +4.1% (p = 0.03), ad revenue = -1.8% (p = 0.08). The PM wants to ship, citing the significant session duration result.
description: Predict the correct ship/no-ship decision and the reasoning behind it.
options: Ship — session duration is statistically significant and a strong proxy for engagement; the OEC result is inconclusive rather than negative.

Do not ship — the pre-registered OEC (completion rate) shows no effect (p = 0.74). The significant session duration is a guardrail metric that was not the basis for the ship decision; shipping based on an unplanned significant guardrail contradicts the pre-registered analysis plan and opens the door to HARKing.
Ship conditionally — require the team to run a follow-up experiment with session duration as the primary metric and ship if it replicates.
Do not ship — ad revenue is down -1.8%, which is close to the -2% guardrail threshold. The risk of a revenue decline outweighs the non-significant OEC result.
explanation: The pre-registered primary metric (OEC) shows no meaningful effect. The ship decision was agreed to be based on the OEC — the whole point of pre-registration is to prevent post-hoc hypothesis selection. Citing the session duration result (a guardrail metric, not the OEC) as the basis to ship is a form of HARKing: the team is selectively reporting the metric that crossed significance after seeing all results. This inflates the effective false-positive rate above the nominal α = 0.05. The p = 0.03 on session duration is not independent evidence — with 3 metrics measured, the probability of at least one crossing 0.05 under the null is roughly 1 - 0.95^3 ≈ 14%. Additionally, the ad revenue guardrail at -1.8% is approaching its -2% threshold, which raises further caution. Option A commits the HARKing error. Option C is a reasonable exploratory path but doesn't address why the current ship decision is invalid. Option D correctly flags the guardrail concern but misidentifies it as the primary reason — the structural problem is the pre-registered OEC null result and the attempted HARKing.
hints: If the OEC was pre-registered as the ship criterion, what does a p = 0.74 on the OEC tell you about the ship decision?
If you test 3 metrics and pick the one that crosses p = 0.05, what is the actual probability of a false positive?

title: Interpret a 95% CI of [−0.1%, +2.1%] on the primary metric
scenario_context: Your experiment completes after 21 days. The primary metric is add-to-cart rate. Result: +1.0% lift, 95% CI: [−0.1%, +2.1%], p = 0.063. The MDE you powered for was 0.8%. The PM asks: 'The CI mostly overlaps with positive territory — can we ship?'
description: Predict the correct interpretation of this result and the appropriate next step.
options: Ship — the CI is 'mostly positive' and the effect is directionally consistent with the MDE. The lower bound is only barely negative.

The result is inconclusive: the CI includes zero, so a null effect is compatible with the data at the 95% confidence level. The p-value (0.063) does not cross the pre-specified α. 'Mostly positive CI' is not a valid decision criterion; shipping on this result introduces a higher-than-agreed false-positive risk.
Do not ship — the result shows the experiment was underpowered. Rerun with a larger sample to narrow the CI.
Ship — p = 0.063 is very close to 0.05. In practice, the difference between p = 0.05 and p = 0.063 is negligible, and business decisions don't require precision at that level.
explanation: A CI that includes zero means a null effect is consistent with the observed data at the stated confidence level. The correct interpretation is inconclusive — not 'directionally positive.' The pre-specified α = 0.05 means you agreed to tolerate a 5% false-positive rate; p = 0.063 does not meet that threshold. 'Mostly positive CI' is informal reasoning that would inflate the actual false-positive rate above 5%. The MDE of 0.8% being inside the CI doesn't change this — the CI tells you about plausible true effects, not about whether the effect is real. Option A commits the error of treating the CI as a majority-vote: 95% of the CI above zero would be borderline convincing, but that's not the same as 'the CI doesn't cross zero.' Option C (rerun) is one valid path if the business case justifies more sample, but it's not required — the correct action is to declare the result inconclusive and decide whether to extend, rerun, or accept the null. Option D is the p-value thresholding fallacy: 0.063 and 0.05 are quantitatively close but the threshold exists precisely to give a pre-committed decision rule; abandoning it post-hoc re-introduces the researcher-degrees-of-freedom problem.
hints: What does it mean for a 95% CI to include zero? Does 'mostly positive' change that meaning?
The pre-specified α was the agreed decision threshold. What is the purpose of pre-specifying it if you deviate post-hoc when the result is close?

title: Team stopped at p = 0.04 on day 3 — why is the result invalid?
scenario_context: A team planned a 14-day experiment with α = 0.05. On day 3, the analyst checks the dashboard and sees p = 0.038 on the primary metric. The team ships that afternoon, citing statistical significance. The feature is reverted 2 weeks later after downstream metrics deteriorate.
description: What is the precise statistical reason the day-3 stop was invalid?
options: The experiment needed 14 days for seasonality reasons; stopping at day 3 misses the weekend-vs-weekday variance that inflates effect sizes on weekdays.

Peeking and stopping at the first p < 0.05 observation inflates the Type I error rate far above the nominal α = 0.05. With continuous monitoring at α = 0.05, the probability of seeing p < 0.05 at least once over a 14-day experiment under the true null is roughly 30–50% — not 5%.
Day 3 is too early for statistical significance to be valid regardless of p-value; significance requires at least 7 days of data to be trustworthy.
The analyst should have used a two-tailed test on day 3; a one-tailed test at that sample size is what inflated the significance.
explanation: The peeking problem is a direct consequence of multiple testing over time. Each time you look at the data and potentially stop, you are performing an additional implicit hypothesis test. Under a true null, the probability of observing p < 0.05 at some point during a 14-day experiment with daily monitoring is approximately 30–50%, not 5% — the actual family-wise Type I error rate is much higher than the nominal α. Stopping at the first significant-looking check exploits the highest-variance point in the experiment (early data has small n, high sampling error) and discards the error-control structure of the planned test. Option A raises a real operational concern (seasonality) but misidentifies it as the primary statistical validity problem. Option C is wrong: there is no minimum-days-for-validity rule; significance can be valid on day 1 if you pre-specified a sequential test with proper alpha spending. The issue is unplanned peeking, not duration per se. Option D misidentifies the test type as the problem — the peeking violation applies regardless of one-tailed vs two-tailed.
hints: If you flip a coin 100 times and stop whenever p < 0.05, how often would you incorrectly reject the null?
What is the difference between a pre-specified interim analysis (as in a sequential design) and an unplanned peek?

title: 5 metrics, 1 significant result — predict the real false-positive rate
scenario_context: A team pre-registers 3 primary metrics (conversion rate, AOV, session duration) and 2 guardrail metrics (report rate, error rate) for a checkout redesign experiment. All 5 are tested at α = 0.05. At the end of 14 days, session duration shows p = 0.041. No other metric shows p < 0.05. The PM prepares to ship citing the session duration result.
description: Predict the actual probability that the session duration finding is a false positive, given the testing setup.
options: 5% — the false-positive rate is exactly α = 0.05 regardless of how many metrics are tested, as long as each test is run at 0.05.

Under no Bonferroni correction, the family-wise error rate across 5 independent tests is approximately 1 − 0.95^5 ≈ 23%. The session duration result (p = 0.041) would need to clear a Bonferroni-corrected threshold of 0.01 to hold a 5% family-wise false-positive rate — it doesn't.
The false-positive rate is lower than 5% because the experiment has 5 chances to find a true effect; more tests increase the chance of finding the real signal.
The false-positive rate is 0.041 — the p-value directly reports the probability this specific result is a false positive.
explanation: When multiple hypotheses are tested simultaneously at the same α, the family-wise error rate (FWER) — the probability of at least one false positive — exceeds α. For 5 independent tests at α = 0.05: FWER ≈ 1 − (1 − 0.05)^5 ≈ 23%. Session duration at p = 0.041 does not clear a Bonferroni-corrected threshold of α/5 = 0.01 (or even α/3 = 0.017 applied only to primary metrics). The result is not publishable as significant under FWER control. The PM should treat session duration as a hypothesis for a follow-up focused experiment. Option A is the naive error: per-test α = 0.05 does not mean family-wise α = 0.05 when tests are conducted simultaneously. Option C inverts the logic — more tests increase false-positive risk, not signal-finding probability (unless you designed the experiment to be underpowered and are adding detection chances, which is a different tradeoff). Option D conflates p-value with posterior probability of false discovery — p-value is not the probability that this specific result is a false positive; it's the probability of seeing this or a more extreme result under the null.
hints: If each of 5 tests has a 5% chance of a false positive, what is the probability that at least one test produces a false positive by chance?
What correction would be needed so that the family-wise false-positive rate is still 5% across all 5 tests?

title: 51.8% control vs 48.2% treatment after 7 days — PM says 'it's just routing, ship it'
scenario_context: You're running a 50/50 A/B test on a homepage feature. After 7 days with 500K users per arm (expected), you observe 518K in control and 482K in treatment (chi-squared p = 4 × 10^-8 against a 50/50 null). The primary metric shows +2.8% lift (p = 0.02). The PM says the imbalance is 'minor routing noise' and wants to ship based on the significant lift.
description: What is the correct next step?
options: Ship — a 3.6% imbalance is operationally minor, the lift is significant, and the SRM is unlikely to affect the direction of the result.

Investigate the SRM root cause before reading any metric. An imbalance this large (chi-squared p = 4 × 10^-8) indicates something systematic is wrong with the randomization — the treatment and control groups may differ on characteristics correlated with the primary metric, making the +2.8% lift estimate unreliable.
Run the experiment for 7 more days and recheck; the SRM may be a transient artifact from the first week and will correct itself with more data.
Apply a 3.6% weighting correction to the treatment arm metrics to normalize for the sample imbalance, then ship if the corrected lift is still significant.
explanation: A chi-squared p-value of 4 × 10^-8 is not routing noise — it is a 8-sigma deviation from the expected 50/50 split. This level of imbalance requires systematic investigation before trusting any metric. Common SRM causes include: assignment service bugs (e.g., sticky sessions overriding random assignment), bot traffic filtered differently between arms, aggressive caching of assignment decisions, or mobile vs desktop traffic routing disparities. Any of these can create selection bias — the 518K control users and 482K treatment users differ not just in count but potentially in composition (e.g., mobile users systematically excluded from treatment). If the groups differ on characteristics correlated with the outcome, the +2.8% lift estimate is biased in an unknown direction. Option A normalizes the problem by calling it 'minor' — a 36K-user imbalance at chi-squared p < 10^-7 is not minor. Option C extends the experiment without addressing the cause — running longer with a broken assignment mechanism produces more biased data. Option D applies a naive weighting correction that addresses the count imbalance but not the compositional bias (if treatment users differ in quality, not just quantity, reweighting by count doesn't fix it).
hints: SRM tells you the randomization assumption may be violated. If the two groups are not exchangeable, what does the lift estimate actually measure?
What types of bugs or system behaviors produce a non-trivial SRM in a well-specified 50/50 randomization?

title: Assignment service has a cookie bug — trace the SRM to its cause and fix
scenario_context: After 5 days of a 50/50 A/B test on a mobile checkout feature, your SRM monitor shows 54.2% in control vs 45.8% in treatment (chi-squared p = 1.3 × 10^-11, expected 50K per arm, observed 54.2K control / 45.8K treatment). Investigation reveals: (a) The assignment service sets a 7-day cookie; (b) Mobile Safari users with 'Prevent Cross-Site Tracking' (ITP) enabled have their cookies deleted after 24 hours; (c) ITP users that return after 24 hours get re-randomized; (d) ITP users make up ~20% of the user base and are skewed toward iOS.
description: Trace how this bug creates SRM and predict the direction of bias in the primary metric.
options: ITP users get re-randomized each day, which increases their total session count across both arms equally — the SRM is caused by a different factor unrelated to ITP.

ITP users who are re-randomized after cookie expiry are more likely to land in control on each re-randomization (50/50 each time), but their re-randomization events inflate the denominator of the control arm count since control users are counted again. The treatment arm underrepresents ITP users relative to their true population share, biasing any iOS-correlated metric toward the control arm.
ITP users re-randomize to treatment at a higher rate because ITP deletion selectively affects the control arm's tracking cookies. This inflates treatment counts.
Re-randomized ITP users appear in both arms simultaneously, creating a within-user crossover that inflates both arms equally.
explanation: ITP users lose their assignment cookie after 24 hours. On re-randomization, they have an equal 50/50 chance of control or treatment — but the key issue is that re-randomization creates additional counting events. Because ITP users return multiple times and get re-randomized each time, their presence in the control arm is counted multiple times when the control arm is defined as 'unique users ever assigned to control.' The net effect: ITP users (iOS-heavy) are systematically underrepresented in the stable treatment group because stable assignment requires a persistent cookie. The 54.2% control vs 45.8% treatment split reflects ITP users inflating the control user count. Primary metric bias direction: if iOS users convert at a different rate than average (common in mobile commerce — iOS users often have higher purchase intent), the treatment arm underrepresents high-converting iOS users, biasing the lift estimate. The direction depends on iOS conversion rate vs average. Option A incorrectly dismisses ITP as the cause. Option C inverts the mechanism — ITP affects both arms' cookie persistence equally at the initial assignment; the bias comes from re-randomization counting inflating the control pool. Option D describes simultaneous dual-arm membership, which isn't what happens with re-randomization.
hints: If ITP users re-randomize every 24 hours, how does 'unique users ever in control' versus 'unique users ever in treatment' evolve over 5 days?
ITP users skew toward iOS. If iOS users convert at a different rate than the population average, how does underrepresenting them in treatment affect the lift estimate?

title: +2.5% significant lift but SRM p = 0.002 — PM wants to ship
scenario_context: A checkout experiment shows +2.5% conversion lift (p = 0.014, 95% CI: [+0.5%, +4.5%]). The SRM check shows chi-squared p = 0.002 (observed: 52.1% control, 47.9% treatment against a 50/50 null). The PM argues: 'The CI is all positive. Even if the SRM biases things, the effect is clearly real and the direction is clear. Ship it.'
description: Evaluate the PM's argument. Is the PM's reasoning valid?
options: Valid — the CI of [+0.5%, +4.5%] is entirely positive, which means the effect is directionally reliable even if the point estimate is biased.

Invalid — SRM with p = 0.002 indicates the randomization assumption is broken. When the groups are not exchangeable, the CI is computed under a false independence assumption and does not bound the true causal effect; a positive CI from a broken experiment tells you nothing reliable about the direction of the true effect.
Partially valid — SRM biases the point estimate but not the sign. If the CI lower bound is well above zero (+0.5%), the sign can be trusted even if the magnitude cannot.

Valid — the SRM is only 2.1 percentage points from balance (52.1% vs 50%), which is operationally minor. At this scale, any bias from SRM would shift the estimate by less than 0.1%, leaving the CI fully positive.
explanation: A 'positive CI' from an experiment with broken randomization does not constitute evidence of a positive causal effect. The CI is a frequentist confidence interval derived under the assumption that treatment and control groups are exchangeable random samples. SRM violates this assumption — the groups may differ systematically on characteristics correlated with conversion (e.g., mobile users, new vs returning, high vs low engagement). When the groups are not comparable, the standard error calculation is wrong, the point estimate is biased, and the CI does not have the stated 95% coverage guarantee. The bias could be large enough to flip the sign — if the 4.2% excess in control consists of high-converting users, the real treatment effect might be negative. You cannot know without investigating the SRM cause. Option C makes the 'CI lower bound > 0 → sign is safe' argument, which fails for exactly the same reason: the CI bounds are only valid under valid randomization. Option D attempts to quantify the bias magnitude at 'less than 0.1%' without any basis — the bias from a 2K-user group imbalance is unknown without knowing the composition difference, and it can be much larger than 0.1% if a high-value segment is misdistributed.
hints: The CI is computed assuming groups are exchangeable random samples. What happens to the CI's coverage guarantee when that assumption is violated?
If the SRM was caused by high-converting users being over-represented in control, what direction would the true lift be?

title: SRM explained by bot traffic filtered differently per arm — which metrics can be salvaged?
scenario_context: You investigate a 53% control / 47% treatment SRM and find the cause: your bot-filtering pipeline runs asynchronously and had a 6-hour lag on day 1. Bots during that window were assigned to treatment before filtering removed them. Post-filtering user counts are balanced (50.1% vs 49.9%). Bot sessions have zero conversion and high page-view counts. The primary metric is conversion rate; secondary is page views per session.
description: After identifying and removing the bot sessions, which metrics are salvageable and which require more scrutiny?
options: Both metrics are fully salvageable once bots are removed from both arms — the post-filtering user counts are balanced, so the experiment is clean.

Conversion rate is likely salvageable after removing bot sessions (bots have zero conversion, so their removal is unlikely to introduce directional bias). Page views per session requires more scrutiny: bots inflate page views in the treatment arm relative to control, and the post-filtering metric distribution may be skewed by the bot-contaminated early period.
Neither metric is salvageable — any experiment with an initial SRM is irreparably compromised and must be restarted regardless of the identified cause.
Page views per session is salvageable (bots inflate it symmetrically in both arms), but conversion rate is not (bots at zero conversion artificially lower the treatment conversion baseline).
explanation: Once you identify the SRM cause and can remove the contaminated sessions cleanly, metrics need to be evaluated on their sensitivity to that specific contamination. Bots were disproportionately in treatment (not control) during the 6-hour window, have zero conversion, and have high page-view counts. For conversion rate: removing zero-conversion bot sessions from treatment slightly raises the treatment conversion rate, but since bots were concentrated early and post-filtering counts are balanced, the direction of bias is known (downward on treatment conversion). The removal should recover a fair estimate. For page views: bots inflate page-view counts in treatment specifically — even after removing bot users, any user-level aggregation that includes the pre-filter window may carry residual contamination from the bot-inflated treatment experience (e.g., bot activity within a session that wasn't fully attributed). Option A overclaims that post-filter balance = clean metrics — the contamination occurred in the metric values during the bot period, not just in user counts. Option C is too conservative — known, bounded SRM causes with clean post-filter data can be addressed; 'restart always' ignores the information available from a diagnosed SRM. Option D inverts the page-view logic: bots were predominantly in treatment, so they inflate page views asymmetrically in treatment, not symmetrically.
hints: Bots were in treatment (not control) for 6 hours. What direction does that push the treatment arm's page views vs conversion rate before and after removal?
If you can identify and remove the contaminated sessions exactly, what residual contamination risk remains in each metric?

title: Cookie-based SRM: novelty-week users drop out of treatment — assess salvageability
scenario_context: Your SRM investigation finds that 9% of treatment users had their assignment cookies deleted during days 1–3 due to an iOS cookie-clearing bug. These users were re-randomized on day 4 and are now counted in both arms across different days. Post-deletion users (days 4–14) are balanced. Conversion rate shows +1.9% lift (p = 0.08) over the full 14 days. A day-4 to day-14 restricted analysis shows +2.4% lift (p = 0.031).
description: Can you use the restricted 10-day analysis to justify shipping?
options: Yes — the restricted analysis avoids the contaminated period and the balanced post-day-4 data gives a valid estimate. Ship based on the restricted result.

The restricted analysis reduces bias from the cookie bug, but it is a post-hoc choice driven by the SRM finding. Pre-specifying an analysis window after identifying an SRM-inflating bug is a legitimate recovery technique only if the window was defined independently of the metric outcomes — here, the window that happens to produce significance was selected after seeing both full-period (p = 0.08) and restricted (p = 0.031) results.
Neither analysis is valid — any SRM, regardless of cause or magnitude, invalidates all analyses from that experiment.
Use the full 14-day result. The restricted analysis has lower sample and is therefore less reliable despite the lower p-value.
explanation: Restricting to the clean post-SRM window is a legitimate technique, but only when the restriction is pre-specified or at least independent of the metric result. Here, the team saw both the full-period (p = 0.08, non-significant) and the restricted result (p = 0.031, significant) and is being tempted to select the significant one. This is a form of data dredging: the SRM window was defined because it happens to produce a significant result. The correct approach: if the restricted window was defined entirely by the SRM cause (days 1–3 had the bug → restrict to days 4–14), and that restriction was committed to before looking at the metric result, the restricted analysis is defensible. If the metric result informed the window choice, the p-value is inflated. The epistemically correct answer is to declare the experiment inconclusive and either rerun or extend with the bug fixed. Option A overclaims that the restricted analysis is automatically valid because the data is clean. Option C is too absolute — diagnosed, bounded SRM causes with clean post-fix data can be partially salvaged with appropriate caution. Option D incorrectly prefers the noisier full-period estimate over a potentially cleaner restricted one on grounds of sample size alone.
hints: Is the decision to use days 4–14 independent of the fact that those days happen to produce significance?
What makes a post-hoc analysis window defensible versus a cherry-picked result?

title: Stratification applied asymmetrically causes SRM — spot and fix
scenario_context: Your team stratifies the experiment by device type to improve balance and reduce variance. Treatment assignment is stratified (50/50 within each device stratum). However, the control assignment uses global randomization (50/50 across the full population without stratification). Result after 10 days: 52.9% control, 47.1% treatment. Mobile constitutes 62% of users; desktop 38%. Mobile users have higher conversion rates (8.2% vs 5.1%).
description: Explain why asymmetric stratification creates SRM and predict the direction of bias in conversion rate.
options: Asymmetric stratification does not cause SRM — the 50/50 splits are specified correctly in each arm. The imbalance must come from a different source.

Asymmetric stratification can cause SRM because global randomization (control) does not guarantee the same device-type proportions as stratified randomization (treatment). If mobile users are assigned slightly differently between the two mechanisms, the arm totals diverge. The direction of bias on conversion depends on which arm has more mobile users: if treatment is under-mobile, it underestimates conversion relative to a balanced sample.
Stratification in one arm and global randomization in the other always produces upward bias in the treatment arm because stratification selects higher-value users into treatment.
The SRM is caused by mobile users refreshing more frequently, which re-randomizes them more often in the global-randomization (control) arm.
explanation: Stratified randomization guarantees device-type proportions within the treatment arm match the population. Global (unstratified) randomization in the control arm produces the correct proportions in expectation but with sampling variance — over a finite sample, this variance can produce a different device-type mix. If mobile users are overrepresented in control (more likely if global randomization draws more mobile users by chance in the early days), the control arm has more high-converting users (mobile: 8.2% conversion), making control look better and underestimating the treatment lift. The SRM check catches the imbalance in total user counts, but the direction of metric bias depends on the device-type distribution within the imbalance. Fix: apply consistent stratification to both arms, or use unstratified randomization in both. Option A incorrectly claims asymmetric stratification can't cause SRM — it can, through differential device-mix realization. Option C incorrectly says stratification selects higher-value users into treatment — stratification selects the population mix correctly; it doesn't select for value. Option D attributes the SRM to refresh behavior, which is not the mechanism here.
hints: Stratified randomization guarantees device proportions; global randomization only guarantees them in expectation. What goes wrong when you mix the two?
Mobile has higher conversion than desktop. If mobile is over-represented in control, which arm looks better?

title: Day-1 lift +8%, day-14 lift +1.5% significant — does this support shipping?
scenario_context: A team tests a redesigned newsfeed algorithm. Daily lift (treatment minus control, conversion rate) over 14 days: Day 1: +8.1%, Day 3: +5.2%, Day 7: +3.1%, Day 14: +1.5% (p = 0.03). The PM argues: 'The effect is decaying but still significant at day 14. We ship the day-14 result.'
description: What is the most important question to answer before accepting the day-14 result as a valid signal?
options: Whether the day-14 lift is large enough to be practically significant — +1.5% at p = 0.03 clears the significance bar, so statistical and practical significance are both satisfied.

Whether the decay pattern is consistent with a novelty effect (users initially curious about the new feed, settling to a lower equilibrium) versus a genuine sustained improvement settling from a volatile launch. A sharp early spike followed by steady decay is the classic novelty signature; if the equilibrium is still declining at day 14, the true long-run effect may be closer to zero or negative.
Whether the experiment has been running long enough — 14 days captures 2 weekends; a further 7-day extension would confirm whether the +1.5% holds.
Whether the p = 0.03 result on day 14 survives a Bonferroni correction for the 14 daily checks.
explanation: The monotonic decay pattern (8.1% → 5.2% → 3.1% → 1.5%) is the hallmark signature of a novelty effect: users engage more intensely with the new feed initially because it is different, and engagement decays as the novelty wears off. The critical question is whether the decay has stabilised or is still declining at day 14. If the trend extrapolates to ~0% by day 21, the day-14 +1.5% is an artifact of the novelty plateau rather than a durable causal effect. A sustained experiment (days 21–28) or a segment analysis comparing new vs returning users would help distinguish novelty from genuine improvement. Option A conflates statistical significance with the absence of a novelty confound — p = 0.03 doesn't tell you whether the effect is real or a diminishing novelty artifact. Option C proposes extending the experiment without identifying why — the extension is only useful if you're looking for decay pattern stabilisation, which should be articulated. Option D raises a valid multiple-testing concern (14 daily looks at p-values) but is secondary to the novelty-effect question; the day-14 read is a pre-specified endpoint, so the daily-look multiple-testing concern is mitigated if the experiment was designed with a single endpoint.
hints: What does a monotonically decaying lift curve over 14 days suggest about the treatment mechanism?
How would you distinguish a novelty effect from a genuine positive effect that happens to be smaller than the initial estimate?

title: High power in week 1 but novelty concern is week 4 — how do you design around this?
scenario_context: Your team tests a new notification system. You're well-powered to detect a 2% lift in 7-day retention at 1 week. However, notification effects are known to decay: users adapt and ignore notifications after 3–4 weeks. Your stakeholder wants a 14-day read but your experiment power analysis shows 80% power at 14 days for a 1.5% MDE. The long-run effect (week 4+) requires 28 days and would drop you to 70% power for a 1% MDE.
description: What is the most defensible experiment design that addresses the novelty concern without sacrificing decision-making speed?
options: Run for 7 days and ship — the 14-day and 28-day reads aren't worth the delay given the business cost.

Run the primary experiment for 14 days with a 1.5% MDE for the ship decision, and simultaneously maintain a smaller holdout group for 28 days to measure long-run retention. Pre-commit to the holdout analysis as a post-ship monitoring signal, not a pre-ship gate.
Run for 28 days — the only valid read on a notification experiment is the week-4+ long-run effect; shorter reads are methodologically unsound.
Segment day-1 to day-7 users as 'novelty exposure' and exclude them from the primary analysis, using only day-8 to day-14 as the clean estimate.
explanation: The 14-day primary experiment addresses the business need for a timely decision (1.5% MDE at 80% power), while the parallel holdout captures the long-run signal without gating the ship decision on a 28-day wait. This is a standard design choice for features where novelty concern is real but business velocity matters: ship with a monitoring holdout rather than delay shipping until the full novelty washout period has passed. The holdout is pre-committed as a monitoring signal (not a gate), which is honest about the uncertainty: if week-4 retention turns negative, the team has the signal to roll back. Option A (7-day ship) ignores the novelty concern entirely and may ship a feature that degrades long-term. Option C (28-day required) is operationally correct for the ideal novelty test but ignores business cost; the question is whether that wait can be justified, and in most product contexts it cannot be the default. Option D (exclude days 1–7) is the wrong adjustment: novelty effects are about new-vs-returning user behavior, not about which days to exclude; excluding early days reduces your sample and doesn't cleanly isolate novelty.
hints: Can you address the novelty concern without making it a pre-ship gate? What monitoring design separates the ship decision from the long-run measurement?
What is the purpose of a holdout group for a feature that has already shipped?

title: New users +6%, returning users +0.2% — which segment has the novelty signature?
scenario_context: A team tests a new homepage design. Segment analysis: New users (first 7 days on platform): +6.1% conversion lift (p = 0.002). Returning users (>30 days on platform): +0.2% conversion lift (p = 0.71). The team has 60K new users and 300K returning users per arm.
description: Predict which segment is most likely to be contaminated by novelty effects, and what the HTE tells you about the decision.
options: New users show the real treatment effect — they haven't formed habits around the old design, so they give a cleaner signal. The returning-user result is attenuated by habit formation.

Returning users show the real long-run effect — the +0.2% represents the treatment's steady-state causal impact after the novelty has worn off. The new-user +6.1% reflects novelty: new users find any new design more engaging than the status quo because they lack a baseline to compare against. The HTE pattern is directionally consistent with a novelty effect dominating the new-user estimate.
