The new-user segment is too small (60K vs 300K) to be reliable; the returning-user result is the only statistically valid estimate and should drive the decision.
The +6.1% in new users is a real long-run effect because new users will constitute the future user base; the returning-user signal should be discounted.
explanation: The new-user segment is the expected locus of novelty bias in a homepage redesign test. New users have no prior experience with the old design, so they are responding to the design in isolation — any difference in engagement reflects both the treatment's causal effect and their initial exploration of the platform. Returning users have baseline expectations calibrated to the old design; when the novelty of a new design wears off, returning users' behavior converges toward their steady-state pattern more quickly than new users. The returning-user +0.2% (non-significant) is the better estimate of the treatment's durable effect for the existing user base. The HTE pattern (large new-user effect, near-zero returning-user effect) is the textbook novelty signature. Option A incorrectly attributes the new-user effect to 'clean signal' — the absence of a prior baseline makes them more susceptible to novelty, not less. Option C dismisses the new-user result on sample size grounds — 60K per arm is substantial; the statistical fragility comes from the returning-user result (non-significant), not the new-user result. Option D makes a business argument ('future user base') that is separate from the statistical novelty question; even if new users matter more long-term, the estimate is still contaminated.
hints: Who lacks a baseline for comparison with the old design — new users or returning users? Who is more likely to find any change 'exciting'?
The returning-user effect is what you'd observe after the novelty period ends. What does it tell you about the long-run causal impact?

title: 12 metrics tested simultaneously, 2 cross p < 0.05 — how many false positives should you expect?
scenario_context: A team runs a single experiment and tests 12 pre-specified metrics simultaneously at α = 0.05. At the end of 14 days, 2 metrics cross p < 0.05: session_duration (p = 0.038) and add_to_cart (p = 0.041). Neither crosses the Bonferroni-corrected threshold of 0.004. The PM wants to ship citing two significant results.
description: How many false positives should you expect from 12 simultaneous tests under the null, and what does that imply about the 2 observed results?
options: You should expect 0 false positives if the team pre-specified the metrics. Pre-registration eliminates the multiple-testing problem.

Under the global null (all metrics truly null), you expect 12 × 0.05 = 0.6 false positives on average. With FWER across 12 tests ≈ 46%, observing 2 results at p < 0.05 is consistent with 0 true positives — both could be false positives. The Bonferroni threshold (p < 0.004 each) is the correct bar for family-wise error control.
2 significant results from 12 tests is strong evidence of true effects — random chance would produce only 0.6, so observing 2 is highly improbable under the null.
The two results are reliable because both p-values are well below 0.05 (0.038 and 0.041); false positives typically appear only near the 0.05 boundary.
explanation: Under the global null, each of 12 tests has a 5% chance of a false positive. Expected false positives = 12 × 0.05 = 0.6. The family-wise error rate is 1 − 0.95^12 ≈ 46%. Observing 2 results at p < 0.05 from 12 tests is not unusual under the null — the expected count is 0.6, and observing 2 is consistent with a moderate unlucky draw (not a 'two is much more than 0.6' argument, because 2 is within a plausible range from a Poisson(0.6) distribution). Neither result clears the Bonferroni threshold (0.004), so neither can be declared significant under family-wise error control. Option A conflates pre-registration with multiple-testing correction. Pre-registration helps prevent HARKing (post-hoc hypothesis selection) but does not eliminate the family-wise error inflation from testing 12 metrics simultaneously. Option C applies the 'expected 0.6, observed 2' comparison incorrectly — Poisson(0.6): P(X ≥ 2) ≈ 12%, which is not 'highly improbable'; it's perfectly consistent with noise. Option D is wrong: false positives are not concentrated near the 0.05 boundary; under the null, p-values are uniformly distributed, so p = 0.038 and p = 0.041 are no less likely to be false positives than p = 0.048.
hints: If each of 12 null tests has a 5% false-positive rate, what is the expected number of false positives across all 12 tests?
What is the family-wise error rate for 12 simultaneous tests at α = 0.05, and what correction restores FWER to 5%?
concepts: TYPE I AND TYPE II ERRORS

title: α = 0.05 when false-positive cost is 10× worse than false-negative cost — what should change?
scenario_context: A team designs an experiment to test a new medical-device calibration algorithm. A false positive (shipping a mis-calibrated algorithm) creates a patient safety risk estimated at $10M. A false negative (failing to ship a genuinely better algorithm) costs $1M in forgone improvement. The team sets α = 0.05 and power = 80% by default.
description: What is wrong with the default α = 0.05 choice, and how should it be adjusted?
options: Nothing is wrong — α = 0.05 is the industry standard and is appropriate for all experimental contexts regardless of the cost asymmetry.

The asymmetric cost structure requires a lower α than 0.05. The cost of a false positive ($10M) is 10× the cost of a false negative ($1M), which argues for a much more conservative threshold (e.g., α = 0.005 or 0.001) to make false positives proportionally rarer. The flip side: a lower α at fixed sample size reduces power, so the team must decide whether to increase sample size to recover power or accept lower power explicitly.
The right response is to lower power (to 50%), not α — since the cost of missing a true effect is low ($1M), it is acceptable to accept high false-negative risk and reduce sample size.
The cost structure calls for a one-tailed test, which halves the effective α and gives conservative control of false positives without requiring a larger sample.
explanation: α and power encode the costs of the two error types. The default α = 0.05 reflects a 5% tolerance for false positives, calibrated for generic research contexts where the cost asymmetry is roughly 1:1. When the cost of a false positive is 10× the cost of a false negative — as in patient safety contexts — the threshold should be much more conservative. Lowering α to 0.005 means false positives are 10× less frequent, aligning the error-rate tradeoff with the cost tradeoff. The consequence is reduced power at fixed sample size; the team must explicitly decide whether to run a larger experiment to recover power (accepting the cost) or to accept lower power (tolerate more false negatives) given the favorable relative cost of false negatives. Option A applies α = 0.05 as context-free doctrine — the whole point of α is that it is a policy choice, not a constant. Option C correctly identifies that false-negative cost is lower but draws the wrong policy conclusion: lowering power to 50% dramatically increases false-negative risk, which is acceptable only when the false-negative cost is very low and the false-positive cost is very high — the team should still be explicit about this tradeoff. Lowering power alone doesn't address the false-positive risk. Option D misapplies one-tailed vs two-tailed: choosing a one-tailed test because it halves the threshold is valid only when you pre-specified a directional alternative; it doesn't substitute for a principled α choice.
hints: α is the maximum tolerated false-positive rate. If a false positive costs 10× more than a false negative, what does that imply about your tolerance for false positives?
What is the mechanical relationship between lowering α and statistical power at a fixed sample size?
concepts: TYPE I AND TYPE II ERRORS

title: CI on DAU: [−50, +2000] — what does this tell you about experiment power?
scenario_context: An experiment tests a new growth feature with primary metric DAU. After 7 days with 40K users per arm, the 95% CI on DAU lift is [−50, +2000] users. The team's MDE was +500 DAU (+1.25%). The PM asks: 'The CI is mostly positive — does this mean we can ship?'
description: Predict what the CI width tells you about experiment power, and whether the PM's conclusion is correct.
options: The CI is mostly positive so shipping is justified — the lower bound is only slightly negative.

A CI of [−50, +2000] with an MDE of +500 tells you the experiment is severely underpowered: the CI is 4× wider than the MDE. The estimate is too imprecise to distinguish a null effect (+0) from a 4× overperformance (+2000). Shipping based on 'mostly positive CI' ignores that the CI lower bound includes meaningful negative territory and the width reflects a very noisy estimate.
The CI width is fine — CI width depends on variance, and DAU naturally has high variance; the team just needs to accept the imprecision.
The CI shows the experiment has sufficient precision because the upper bound (+2000) is 4× the MDE — this indicates the treatment has strong upside potential.
explanation: A CI width of 2050 users on a metric where the MDE is 500 means you have roughly 4× less precision than needed. In power-analysis terms, you are severely underpowered: at this variance and sample size, even a true null effect could produce a CI that 'mostly positive' — the noise swamps the signal. The point estimate is somewhere in [−50, +2000] with the center likely around +975, which is statistically consistent with both zero and +2000. Shipping requires knowing the effect is real, not just that the CI's center happens to be above zero. Option A applies the 'mostly positive CI' heuristic, which is only valid when the CI is narrow enough that the lower bound is meaningfully above zero. Option C is correct that DAU has high variance, but 'accept the imprecision' is not a reason to ship — it's a reason to run a larger or longer experiment, or to use CUPED to reduce variance. Option D misreads the CI: the upper bound being large means the experiment is noisy, not that the treatment has strong upside. A wide CI upper bound reflects uncertainty, not evidence of effect magnitude.
hints: How does the CI width compare to the MDE? What does it mean when your uncertainty interval is 4× larger than the effect you were trying to detect?
Can a 'mostly positive CI' be consistent with a true null effect? Under what conditions?

title: CI hasn't narrowed after 3 weeks — what's the root cause?
scenario_context: A team runs an experiment on a low-frequency product event (quarterly subscription renewal). After 3 weeks with 80K users per arm, the 95% CI on renewal rate lift is [−1.2%, +3.8%]. At week 1 the CI was [−2.1%, +5.3%] — it has narrowed slightly but is still wide. The PM asks why more data isn't helping more.
description: What is the most likely root cause, and what is the appropriate action?
options: The CI hasn't narrowed enough because 3 weeks is insufficient to observe quarterly renewal events — users renew on a 3-month cycle, so most users in the experiment haven't reached their renewal date yet. More data over a longer time period (not more users over the same time) is the solution.
The CI hasn't narrowed because the sample size is still insufficient — add more users per arm and the CI will narrow proportionally.
The CI is correct and reflects that the true effect is small — the CI is converging on the true effect and will stabilize near zero.
The CI width reflects measurement error in the renewal tracking system — fix the tracking pipeline first.
explanation: Quarterly renewal is a low-frequency event: in a 3-week window, most users have not yet reached their renewal date. The CI is wide not because of insufficient users (80K per arm is substantial) but because the metric has very low occurrence rate — most observations are zeros. Adding more users to a 3-week window doesn't help if those users also haven't reached their renewal date. The solution is to extend the experiment duration until a meaningful fraction of users reach their renewal cycle (12+ weeks). This is a metric-frequency problem: the relevant event hasn't happened yet for most users, so the effective sample size on the metric is a small fraction of the enrolled users. Option B incorrectly diagnoses the problem as sample size — adding users helps when variance is the bottleneck; here, the bottleneck is event occurrence rate, which is fixed by time, not user count. Option C would be correct if the metric had high occurrence rate and the CI were stable — but here the CI is still wide because there's almost no observed outcome data yet. Option D (tracking error) is possible in general but is not supported by the scenario description and is secondary to the event-frequency diagnosis.
hints: If most users in a 3-week experiment haven't yet reached their quarterly renewal date, what fraction of your data actually contains the outcome event?
What is the difference between 'not enough users' and 'not enough time for the event to occur'?

title: CI [+1%, +5%] clears the MDE of 3% — should you ship?
scenario_context: Your experiment on a search algorithm returns: +3.1% lift on click-through rate, 95% CI [+1.0%, +5.2%], p = 0.003. The pre-specified MDE was 3%. The CI lower bound (+1%) is below the MDE. The PM argues 'the effect is significant and the center is above the MDE — clear ship.' Your data science lead argues 'the lower bound is below the MDE — so we can't confirm the effect is above our bar.'
description: Whose reasoning is correct, and what does the MDE mean in this context?
options: The PM is right — the center of the CI (+3.1%) is above the MDE and the result is significant. Statistical significance plus a meaningful point estimate is the correct ship criterion.

The data science lead is applying the MDE incorrectly. MDE is a power-analysis input — the smallest effect you could reliably detect — not a minimum effect required for shipping. The correct ship criterion is whether the effect is statistically significant (yes, p = 0.003) and practically meaningful (yes, +3.1% CTR lift is the expected OEC response). The CI lower bound being below the MDE is not a no-ship signal.
Neither is right — you need to extend the experiment until the CI lower bound exceeds the MDE to confirm the effect is above the minimum bar.
The data science lead is right — if the CI overlaps with values below the MDE, you cannot confirm the effect size meets the bar set for shipping.
explanation: MDE is a design parameter, not a minimum-effect-size requirement for shipping. It answers the question 'what is the smallest effect we would want to reliably detect given our sample size?' — it is the power-analysis input used to size the experiment. It does not set a minimum effect required to be present for the ship decision. The correct ship criteria are: (1) statistically significant (p = 0.003 — yes), (2) directionally positive (yes), (3) practically meaningful (the team must define this based on business impact — +3.1% CTR is large by industry norms). The CI lower bound (+1%) being below the MDE (3%) tells you that the true effect could be as small as +1% — but if +1% CTR is still worthwhile to ship (even if smaller than what you powered for), it's not a reason to hold. The data science lead is correct that the lower bound is below the MDE, but the conclusion 'therefore don't ship' is wrong — that confuses MDE with a minimum-required-effect. Option A is partially right but the reasoning ('center above MDE') is not the canonical framing. Option C imposes a non-standard bar (CI lower bound > MDE) that would require unnecessarily large experiments. Option D correctly states the CI lower bound issue but incorrectly applies it as a no-ship rule.
hints: What does MDE mean in the context of power analysis, and what does it mean in the context of the ship decision?
If the true effect could be +1% (CI lower bound), is that necessarily a reason not to ship, or is it a question of whether +1% is still worthwhile?

title: CUPED reduces variance by 30% — what happens to your experiment duration?
scenario_context: Your team's revenue experiment requires 14 days to achieve 80% power at a 2% MDE. Your stats team applies CUPED using 7-day pre-experiment revenue as the covariate, reducing metric variance by 30%. The PM asks: 'Do we still need 14 days?'
description: Predict how CUPED's 30% variance reduction affects the required experiment duration.
options: Duration stays at 14 days — CUPED reduces variance but doesn't change the required sample size for a given power level.

Required sample size is proportional to variance. A 30% variance reduction means the required n drops by 30% (new n = 0.70 × old n). If daily accrual is constant, the required duration also drops by 30% — from 14 days to approximately 10 days.
Duration drops by 30% only if accrual is the bottleneck. If daily accrual is seasonal and the 14-day period includes low-traffic weekends, the true reduction in duration is smaller.
CUPED reduces variance by 30% in metric terms but power also depends on effect size; unless the true effect size changes, power stays the same and 14 days is still required.
explanation: Required sample size for a fixed-horizon test is proportional to variance (n ∝ σ²/δ² at fixed α and power). Reducing σ² by 30% reduces the required n by 30%. If daily user accrual is constant, duration is proportional to n, so the experiment duration falls from 14 days to approximately 14 × 0.70 ≈ 10 days. This is the primary practical benefit of CUPED: it effectively buys experiment throughput by reducing the variance per observation without collecting more data. Option A is wrong: variance reduction directly reduces the required n, which is the whole point of CUPED. Option C is partially true — if accrual has temporal variation (weekends vs weekdays), the relationship between n and calendar days is not strictly linear; but the question asks about the directional effect, and the 30% reduction is the correct first-order answer. Option D confuses the formula: n ∝ σ²/δ² — reducing σ² at fixed δ directly reduces n and therefore duration. The effect size δ doesn't change because CUPED doesn't alter the treatment; it only removes pre-experiment variance from the residual.
hints: The formula for required sample size contains σ² in the numerator. What happens to the required n when σ² decreases by 30%?
If required n drops by 30% and daily accrual is constant, how does that translate to calendar days?

title: Positive HTE on mobile, negative on desktop — how do you control false discovery rate before acting?
scenario_context: A search redesign experiment shows: overall lift: +1.8% (p = 0.09, not significant). Segment analysis: mobile users (60% of traffic) +3.2% lift (p = 0.021), desktop users (40% of traffic) −1.1% lift (p = 0.31). The PM wants to ship to mobile only.
description: What is the correct statistical treatment before acting on the segment finding?
options: Ship to mobile — p = 0.021 is below 0.05, and the mobile segment is 60% of traffic. The segment result is statistically valid.

The mobile segment finding is a post-hoc subgroup analysis. With at least 2 segments tested (mobile and desktop), the family-wise error rate is inflated. Bonferroni-corrected threshold for 2 subgroups is p < 0.025; p = 0.021 barely clears this but the overall result is non-significant — this pattern is inconsistent with a real effect and is likely a false positive. The correct action is to pre-specify mobile as the primary population in a follow-up experiment and replicate.
The segment finding is valid — Bonferroni correction only applies to unrelated hypotheses; mobile and desktop segments are naturally complementary, so no correction is needed.
The non-significant overall result means the experiment is underpowered; the mobile segment result may be detecting a true effect that the full-population analysis missed.
explanation: Subgroup analyses on non-pre-specified segments require multiple-testing correction even when the segments are 'complementary.' Mobile and desktop are 2 tests on the same data; the FWER across 2 tests at α = 0.05 is 1 − 0.95^2 ≈ 9.75%. The Bonferroni threshold for 2 tests is 0.025. p = 0.021 barely passes this threshold, but the pattern raises further concern: the overall result is non-significant (p = 0.09) while a subgroup is significant. This is an inconsistency — if the overall population has no detectable effect, a subgroup detection is more likely to reflect a false positive (one of the segments happened to go positive by noise). The correct response is to treat the mobile segment as a hypothesis and pre-register it for a follow-up focused experiment. Option A applies uncorrected per-segment α = 0.05, which does not control FWER. Option C is wrong: the correction applies regardless of whether segments are complementary — the correlation structure between tests affects the precision of the FWER estimate, not whether correction is needed at all. Option D conflates underpowering with subgroup signal: a non-significant overall result with a significant subgroup is a flag for HTE, but the statistical validity of the subgroup result still depends on proper correction.
hints: If you test 2 segments simultaneously at α = 0.05, what is the probability that at least one crosses significance under the null?
The overall population result is non-significant but a subgroup is significant. Is this pattern more consistent with a true heterogeneous effect or a false positive?

title: 2 unplanned metrics added after seeing early results — identify the problem
scenario_context: A team pre-registers 3 metrics for a checkout A/B test: conversion rate (primary), AOV (guardrail), and refund rate (guardrail). On day 5, the analyst sees conversion rate is lagging and adds 2 new metrics to the dashboard: add-to-cart rate and session-to-purchase time. At experiment end, conversion rate shows p = 0.18; add-to-cart rate shows p = 0.032; session-to-purchase time shows p = 0.041.
description: Identify the core problem and the correct way to handle the add-to-cart finding.
options: No problem — the team can add metrics at any time during an experiment. Adding metrics that show significance is standard exploratory analysis.

Adding metrics after observing early trending data is HARKing: the new metrics were added because the original primary metric was not moving, which means they were selected with implicit knowledge of the data. The add-to-cart p = 0.032 is not a pre-registered result and should not be treated as a confirmatory finding. It is a hypothesis for a follow-up experiment.

The problem is that add-to-cart rate and session-to-purchase time were not in the original pre-registration, so they should have been excluded from the analysis entirely — they cannot be reported at all.
The only issue is multiple testing: apply Bonferroni to all 5 metrics (3 original + 2 added) and the threshold becomes 0.01; since neither new metric clears 0.01, they are non-significant.
explanation: Adding metrics after observing partial results exploits researcher degrees of freedom: the analyst saw that conversion rate wasn't moving and searched for a metric that did. This is a form of p-hacking — the probability of finding at least one of many possible metrics at p < 0.05 is much higher than 5% when the choice is informed by early data. The add-to-cart result is therefore not confirmatory; it's an exploratory finding that requires replication in a focused experiment where add-to-cart is the pre-specified primary. Option A is wrong: adding metrics with implicit knowledge of early data direction is never 'standard exploratory analysis' in a confirmatory experiment — it inflates the false-positive rate. Option C is too restrictive: post-hoc metrics can be reported as exploratory and as hypotheses for follow-up, but they should not be presented as confirmatory evidence. Option D partially addresses the problem with a Bonferroni correction but misses the deeper issue: the multiple-testing correction controls for random multiple comparisons, not for the selection of which metrics to test based on trending data (which is a different, harder-to-correct bias).
hints: Were the two new metrics added because the primary metric wasn't moving? How does that change the interpretation of their significance?
What is the difference between pre-registered confirmatory analysis and post-hoc exploratory analysis in terms of what you can claim from the result?

title: Predict which input change most efficiently reduces required sample size
scenario_context: Your current experiment requires n = 125,000 per arm (250K total) for 80% power, α = 0.05, MDE = 2%, metric σ = 15%. The PM asks if you can reduce required sample size by any of: (A) increasing power to 90%, (B) increasing MDE to 3%, (C) reducing σ by 25% via CUPED, or (D) increasing α to 0.10.
description: Rank options B, C, D by their proportional reduction in required sample size (option A increases n — eliminate it first).
options: D > C > B: increasing α to 0.10 gives the largest proportional reduction, then CUPED, then widening the MDE.

B > C > D: widening MDE to 3% gives the largest reduction (n ∝ 1/MDE²; a 50% MDE increase halves n squared, reducing n by 75%). CUPED (25% σ reduction) reduces n by ~44% (n ∝ σ², so 0.75² = 0.56). Raising α to 0.10 from 0.05 reduces n by roughly 10–15%.
C > D > B: CUPED gives the largest reduction because variance reduction has a quadratic effect; raising α is second; widening MDE is smallest because the MDE was already appropriate.
All three changes have equal effect on sample size — they all reduce the required n by approximately the same proportion.
explanation: Required sample size ∝ (z_α/2 + z_β)² × σ² / δ². Working through each option at fixed power=80%: Option B (MDE 2%→3%, a 50% increase in δ): n ∝ 1/δ², so new n = old n × (2/3)² = old n × 4/9 ≈ 44% of original — a 56% reduction. Option C (σ reduced by 25% via CUPED): n ∝ σ², so new n = old n × (0.75)² = 0.5625 × old n — a 44% reduction. Option D (α 0.05→0.10): z_α/2 changes from 1.96 to 1.645; the effect on n is approximately (1.645 + 0.842)²/(1.96 + 0.842)² ≈ (2.487)²/(2.802)² ≈ 79% of original — a 21% reduction. Rank: B (56%) > C (44%) > D (21%). Option B wins because MDE enters n as an inverse square — doubling MDE quarters n. Option A correctly eliminates raising power (increases n). Option C incorrectly puts CUPED first — variance reduction is powerful, but a 25% σ reduction is a 44% n reduction, not as large as a 50% MDE change. Option D incorrectly puts CUPED first with an incorrect explanation.
hints: Sample size is proportional to σ²/δ². If MDE (δ) increases by 50%, how does n change? If σ decreases by 25%, how does n change?
Which parameter appears in n as an inverse square — MDE or σ? Which appears as a direct square?

title: PM wants to halve experiment duration — what must change and what are the tradeoffs?
scenario_context: Your team's planned experiment is 14 days at 80% power for a 2% MDE on conversion rate. The PM says: 'We need results in 7 days. How do we make that work?' Daily user accrual is fixed (not under your control). The metric is not amenable to CUPED (no strong pre-experiment covariate).
description: What must change to ship a valid experiment in 7 days, and what is the honest tradeoff statement to the PM?
options: Nothing needs to change — 7 days is sufficient as long as the experiment reaches significance before the deadline.

Halving the duration halves the sample size, which reduces power. To maintain 80% power in 7 days, the MDE must increase to approximately 2√2 ≈ 2.83% — you can only detect effects that are 41% larger than originally planned. Alternatively, accept lower power (e.g., 60%) at the original 2% MDE and accept higher false-negative risk. The PM must choose between a wider MDE or lower power — there is no free compression.
Run for 7 days but use a one-tailed test instead of two-tailed — this effectively halves the alpha and compensates for the reduced sample size.
7 days is fine — extend the analysis to include a 7-day pre-period as pseudo-control data to double the effective sample.
explanation: Halving the duration halves the sample (n ∝ duration at fixed daily accrual). Required n ∝ 1/δ² at fixed power and α. To keep power at 80% with half the sample: δ_new² = δ_old² / 0.5, so δ_new = δ_old × √2 ≈ 2 × 1.41 = 2.83%. Alternatively, keeping MDE at 2% but halving n: power drops from 80% to roughly 60–65% (the exact value depends on the z-score arithmetic). Either tradeoff is real — the PM is asking for something that costs precision. The correct communication: 'At 7 days we can detect 2.83% lift at 80% power, or we can keep 2% MDE but accept ~62% power. Which tradeoff is acceptable given the business cost of a false negative?' Option A is the classic peeking error: stopping when the experiment 'reaches significance' before the planned duration inflates Type I error. Option C applies a one-tailed test to compensate for reduced sample — but a one-tailed test is a hypothesis choice, not a sample-size substitute; it requires a pre-specified directional alternative and doesn't add data. Option D using pre-period data as pseudo-control is invalid — pre-period observations are not randomized and conflate time trends with treatment effects.
hints: If you halve the sample size, how does that change the MDE you can detect at fixed power? Use the fact that n ∝ 1/δ².
What is the honest tradeoff the PM needs to accept — and why can't you compress duration without cost?

title: What is the difference between 'insufficient power' and 'metric structurally too rare to detect'?
scenario_context: An e-commerce platform tests a post-purchase survey prompt. Primary metric: survey completion rate (overall: 0.3% of sessions). After 60 days and 2M sessions per arm, the CI on lift is [−0.04%, +0.12%]. A parallel experiment on a high-frequency metric (session_start: 95% of sessions) with the same 2M sessions per arm shows CI [−0.8%, +2.1%]. The team says: 'The survey experiment was underpowered; we need more time.'
description: Is 'underpowered' the correct diagnosis for the survey metric, or is there a more precise characterisation?
options: Underpowered is correct — the 60-day experiment hasn't accumulated enough events for the survey metric. More time will fix it.

The more precise diagnosis is low metric sensitivity due to low event frequency. Survey completion at 0.3% means the metric has very low occurrence rate — even at 2M sessions, you observe only ~6,000 survey completions per arm. The variance of a rare-event metric is dominated by the scarcity of events, not by session count. Adding more sessions without increasing the event rate adds mostly uninformative zeros. The correct fix is to either change the metric definition (e.g., survey impressions) or accept that this metric is structurally undetectable at reasonable sample sizes.
Underpowered and low event frequency are the same diagnosis — both are fixed by more data.
The experiment is correctly powered — the CI [−0.04%, +0.12%] is narrow and any true effect would be detected. The treatment simply has no effect on survey completion.
explanation: Underpowering and low metric sensitivity from rare events are related but distinct. Underpowering means you have insufficient sample for the metric's variance and the target MDE — more data fixes it. Rare-event metrics (0.3% occurrence) have a structural problem: the metric variance is inversely proportional to the event frequency, and for a 0.3%-rate metric, you need roughly (σ²_rare / σ²_common) × more sessions than a high-frequency metric. At 0.3%, variance = p(1-p) ≈ 0.003; at 95%, variance ≈ 0.0475 — but the rare metric has far fewer actual events (6K vs 1.9M), meaning the standard error of the proportion is driven by (1/√n_events), where n_events is tiny. 'More sessions over the same time' helps marginally, but the required sample may be orders of magnitude larger than what's feasible. This is a metric definition problem: if you care about post-purchase feedback, you need a metric that is measurable at your sample size (e.g., survey completion rate among users who saw the prompt). Option A treats this as a standard underpowering problem fixable by more time — it's not; the event rate is the bottleneck. Option C incorrectly conflates the two concepts. Option D misreads the CI as 'narrow' — [−0.04%, +0.12%] is narrow in absolute terms but huge relative to the 0.3% baseline.
hints: If 0.3% of sessions complete the survey, how many survey completion events do you actually observe in 2M sessions? Is that enough to estimate a rate precisely?
What determines the variance of a proportion — the denominator (sessions) or the numerator (events)? What happens when the numerator is tiny?

title: Product has 50K DAU; power analysis requires 200K per arm — what are your options?
scenario_context: You want to detect a 1% lift on conversion rate (σ = 18%) with 80% power, α = 0.05. Sample size calculation: 200,000 users per arm, 400,000 total. Your product has 50,000 DAU. At that accrual rate, you'd need 8 days per arm — but the experiment design requires all users on a given day to be in one arm (geo-level randomization). You have 3 geo-regions.
description: Which option most efficiently addresses the sample-size-vs-accrual constraint?
options: Run user-level randomization instead of geo-level — this gives 50K × 8 days = 400K users quickly.

Widen the MDE: detect 2% instead of 1%. Required n drops by 75% (n ∝ 1/MDE²), reducing the sample requirement from 200K to 50K per arm. This is achievable in 1 day of geo-level randomization per arm if all 3 regions are used.
Extend the experiment to 4 weeks — this accumulates 50K × 28 = 1.4M users across all geos, well exceeding the 400K total required.
Use a Bayesian approach to set a looser credible interval standard — this reduces the required sample by accepting higher posterior uncertainty.
explanation: With geo-level randomization and only 3 regions, user-level randomization (Option A) is specified as infeasible — the constraint is geo-level assignment, not just accrual. The most practical fix is to reconsider the MDE. At 2% MDE: n ∝ 1/δ², so new n = 200K × (1/2)² = 50K per arm — achievable in 1 geo-day. The business question is whether a 2% lift is still worth detecting and acting on; if yes, this is the correct tradeoff. Option A violates the geo-level randomization constraint (which exists, presumably, to handle network effects or regional policy consistency). Option C accumulates 1.4M users across all geos over 28 days — but with only 3 geo-regions rotating assignment, this means each geo is in treatment or control for 9+ days with very few independent randomization units (geos, not users); the effective sample size for inference is 3 geos, not 1.4M users. Geo-level experiments are limited by the number of geos, not the number of users within geos. Option D (Bayesian / loose credible interval) doesn't address the randomization-unit constraint and conflates accepting uncertainty with solving the accrual problem.
hints: In a geo-level randomization with 3 regions, what is the effective sample size for inference — the number of users or the number of geos?
If MDE doubles (1% → 2%), how does required n change? Is the resulting sample achievable given the geo constraint?

title: High-variance metric vs low-variance metric: when does the choice materially harm power?
scenario_context: A team needs to test a pricing change. Two candidate primary metrics: (A) revenue per session (σ = $42, mean = $8.20, CV = 5.1) driven by heavy-purchaser tail; (B) conversion rate (σ = 0.17, mean = 0.12, CV = 1.4). The MDE they want to detect is a 3% relative lift. The power analysis shows: metric A requires 1.8M sessions per arm; metric B requires 65K sessions per arm. Daily traffic is 200K sessions.
description: What should the team choose as primary metric, and how should the high-variance metric be used?
options: Use revenue per session (A) as primary — it directly measures business impact; conversion rate is a proxy.

Use conversion rate (B) as primary and revenue per session as a guardrail. The 28× difference in required sample (1.8M vs 65K per arm) is driven by revenue's fat-tailed distribution (CV = 5.1 vs 1.4). The team can reach 80% power in under 1 week on conversion rate, versus 9+ days on revenue. Revenue should still be monitored as a guardrail to confirm no revenue degradation.
Run two separate experiments — one powered for each metric — to get independent reads.
Apply a log transformation to revenue per session; log-revenue has much lower variance and would close most of the sample size gap.
explanation: METRIC SENSITIVITY is the core issue: revenue per session has a coefficient of variation 3.6× higher than conversion rate (5.1 vs 1.4), producing a sample requirement 28× larger. With 200K daily sessions, the revenue primary metric requires 9+ days per arm, which is operationally costly and creates novelty-effect risk. Conversion rate directly measures whether the pricing change drives purchase decisions — the first-order effect of a pricing test — and reaches 80% power in about 7 hours per arm at 65K × 2 / 200K ≈ 0.65 days. Using revenue as a guardrail is the right complementary position: it monitors whether conversion gains translate to revenue (they might not, if the pricing change increases conversions but decreases AOV). Option A is incorrect because revenue per session is a valid business metric but a terrible experiment metric given its variance structure. Option C (two experiments) doubles the experiment cost and introduces multiple-testing complications without solving the underlying metric-selection problem. Option D (log transformation) is a useful variance-reduction technique — log-revenue is much better behaved — but it changes the metric's interpretation (you'd be measuring relative lifts in log-revenue, not absolute revenue) and still has meaningfully higher variance than conversion rate.
hints: The CV (coefficient of variation = σ/mean) captures how much relative noise a metric has. How does CV = 5.1 vs 1.4 translate into the 28× difference in required sample size?
What role should the high-variance metric play in the experiment if it can't be the primary metric at a feasible sample size?
